entries.title: White Sox ace Davis Martin 'out of whack' in rare stinker
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> ace <b>Davis Martin </b>had been feeling it for weeks. He entered the game Tuesday against the Twins having allowed one run or fewer in seven of his last eight starts, going no less than 5⅔ innings in any of them.</p><p>But the only thing he felt Tuesday was ‘‘out of whack.’’</p><p>Martin (8-2) allowed season highs of six runs, 10 hits and three walks, and the Sox dropped their second consecutive game, losing 6-4. The series finale Wednesday will be their 13th game in a row without a day off. By the looks of it, they could use one.</p><p>‘‘You can talk about trying to get ahead of guys a little better,’’ Martin said, ‘‘but at the end of the day, it wasn’t my day.’’</p><p>Martin has been the Sox’ stopper. They entered 6-0 in games he had started after a loss. They even took a 3-0 lead in the third on <b>Luisangel Acuna’s</b> aggressiveness — after drawing a walk, he stole second and third and scored on a catcher <b>Alex Jackson’s</b> throwing error — and <b>Miguel Vargas’</b> two-run single.</p><p>But Martin unraveled in the fourth, allowing four runs, five hits and a walk. He left with two outs in the fifth after allowing another run.</p><p>‘‘We’re not landing the curveballs early,’’ Martin said. ‘‘I need to be better about dropping in curveballs. Mixing pitches, mixing speeds — that’s what makes me good. Just didn’t have a feel for it. You’re gonna have some of these starts.’’</p><p>Martin didn’t get enough help from his defense, either. In the third, rookie first baseman <b>Jacob Gonzalez </b>broke to field a bunt that Martin was handling and couldn’t get back to the bag in time. And the Twins were aggressive on the bases, running on rookie left fielder <b>Sam Antonacci </b>to score while trail runners took an extra base.</p><p>‘‘Some tough plays there,’’ manager <b>Will Venable</b> said. ‘‘The one with Jacob, he wants to be aggressive. Just gotta have a feel for where Davis is at. . . . We’ve gotta do everything we can to not let trail runners advance, especially with how infrequently guys are thrown out. The plays that we’ll talk about, we’ll clean up.’’</p><p>Acuna stole another base in the eighth, becoming the first Sox player to steal three bags in a game since <b>Juan Pierre</b> on Sept. 30, 2010. He has 11 steals for the year.</p><h3>Rare ‘two-out play’</h3><p>The Sox made history Monday, turning a double play that wasn’t scored a double play.</p><p>With one out in the third and <b>Brooks Lee </b>on first, <b>Kody Clemens </b>grounded to first baseman Gonzalez, who threw to shortstop <b>Colson Montgomery</b> at second to retire Lee. But Montgomery’s throw back to first sailed over Gonzalez’s head.</p><p>Gonzalez recovered the ball and threw back to second to nab Clemens. Though the throw was a two-hopper, it was on target and in time to get him.</p><p>Gonzalez, a rookie being pressed into first-base duty with <b>Munetaka Murakami </b>(hamstring) on the injured list, drew praise from Venable.</p><p>‘‘I gave him some love on it, for sure,’’ Venable said. ‘‘It was a cool play. A lot of confidence to make both of those throws. Made really good throws, too. It was cool to see him execute it.’’</p><h3>‘Winning Ugly’ reunion</h3><p>It has been 43 years since the ‘‘Winning Ugly’’ Sox won the American League West with 99 victories. That isn’t a nice round number usually associated with anniversaries, but it won’t stop the club from celebrating the 1983 team with a reunion before the game June 27 against the Royals.</p><p>Players, coaches and staff from the team, which gave Sox fans their first taste of postseason baseball since the 1959 World Series squad, will be on hand, including fan favorites <b>Harold Baines</b>, <b>Carlton Fisk</b>, <b>Ron Kittle</b>, <b>Rudy Law </b>and <b>Greg Luzinski</b>.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-4a0005" name="list-4a0005"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, pageNumber=1, inverseColors=false, footerBgColor=#000000, bodyFont=font-3, showListNumbers=false, imagePositionHorizontal=null, rteBodyFont=font-3, headerBottomBorderColor=#111010, items=[{type=Image, url=https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/06/02/sean-burke-thank-god-i-get-to-play-for-the-chicago-white-sox-randal-grichuk-chris-getz, authors=[{authorPageUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/jeff-agrest, media=[{alt=11-20-stewart-agrest-2-0.jpg, ampLink=null, _styledTemplate=null, _template=/image/Image.hbs, image={src=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/aa/7e/6765027c315652b7137576f04898/11-20-stewart-agrest-2-0.jpg, width=512, height=512}, narrowImage={src=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/aa/7e/6765027c315652b7137576f04898/11-20-stewart-agrest-2-0.jpg, width=512, height=512}}], ampLink=null, _styledTemplate=null, bio=[{items=[Jeff Agrest is deputy sports editor at the Chicago Sun-Times.]}], _template=/author/byline/AuthorByline.hbs, name=[{items=[Jeff Agrest]}], jobTitle=[{items=[Deputy sports editor]}]}], description=[{items=[The Sox right-hander didn’t mean it religiously, but he meant it nonetheless. entries.title: 2 shot in Washington Heights
entries.summary: <p>Two people were hospitalized after a shooting in Washington Heights Tuesday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>A man, 29, was on the sidewalk in the 400 block of West 98th Street at 7:30 p.m. when he was shot in the chest, police said. He was taken to Christ Medical Center in critical condition.</p><p>Another man, 55, was shot in the neck there and took himself to Little Company of Mary Hospital, where he was listed in critical condition, according to police.</p><p>No one is in custody, police said.<br></p>

entries.title: Man charged with DUI in fatal Kennedy Expy. crash
entries.summary: <p>A man has been charged with DUI after a crash on the Kennedy Expressway near the West Loop that killed two people in March, according to Illinois State Police.</p><p>Isaiah Olivas, 27, faces charges of two counts of aggravated driving under the influence involving death and two counts of aggravated driving under the influence causing great bodily harm, state police said. He turned himself in to police Monday.</p><p>At 1:46 a.m. March 15, Olivas hit a sedan that was broken down in the left lane of I-90 southbound near Randolph Street, state police said. Two of the sedan’s occupants, Rashad Dean and Nadinah Cunnings, later died.</p><p>Olivas and the other two sedan passengers were also hospitalized, state police said.</p><p>Olivas was ordered held at a detention hearing, according to state police.</p>

entries.title: Sky can’t match energy of Mystics’ youth movement
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON — Mystics coach Sydney Johnson said before the game Tuesday that he was worried about the Sky’s experience, given their roster full of seasoned, accomplished players.</p><p>The Mystics, by contrast, have the youngest roster in the WNBA. They feature eight rookies and are as focused on player development as they are on winning.</p><p>Still, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> (3-6) couldn’t keep up. They let the young’uns give them the business and dropped their fifth consecutive game with a 90-72 loss.</p><p>The Mystics’ rookies announced themselves early and often, with five scoring in the first half. Forward Shakira Austin, an elder at 25, continued her dominant stretch with 17 points and eight rebounds. And former Sky guard Michaela Onyenwere made her old team pay with 13 points on 5-for-6 shooting.</p><p>By the fourth quarter, with the game out of hand, the fans chanted for the only rookie who hadn’t yet made an appearance: 5-6 guard Rori Harmon.</p><p>They got their wish. The youth revolution is fully under way in Washington.</p><p>The Sky simply had no answer for it. Despite defense being their calling card. Despite the Mystics playing without their leading scorer, Sonia Citron.</p><p>Then again, the Sky are no picture of health themselves. They’ve spent the whole season short-handed, and it has chipped away at their defensive identity. The loss of forward Rickea Jackson to a season-ending torn ACL looms over every loss. Even a week without rookie wing Gabriela Jaquez has hurt them badly.</p><p>‘‘We started off [the season] really strong,’’ guard Natasha Cloud said of the defense. ‘‘Obviously, losing some players, not having players, you have to adjust and pivot and find where you’re gonna piece in and plug in.’’</p><p>Clearly, they’re still figuring it out. Ball-screen coverage took a step back against the Mystics. Rebounding remains a massive issue. The Sky lost the rebounding battle 46-29, and the Mystics turned the extra chances into 17 points.</p><p>Offense remains a problem, too. After taking great care of the ball in the first few games, the Sky turned it over more than 17 times for the second consecutive game. Coach Tyler Marsh said teams are being more physical, making them extend their offense further out. But something just isn’t clicking.</p><p>The Sky tried a few new looks defensively, flashing a full-court press for the first time and switching to a zone in the third quarter. But the zone only freed up wide-open three-pointers for the Mystics.</p><p>After the Sky dropped their fourth game in a row last week, Marsh said the locker room was disappointed but not dejected. The dejection hung in the air Tuesday, plain for everyone to see.</p><p>‘‘[We need to] be better when times get hard,’’ guard Sydney Taylor said. ‘‘Don’t put our heads down. I think body language on our team is an issue at times. I guess you could say myself included.’’</p><p>There were still bright spots. Kamilla Cardoso had a double-double with 12 points and 13 rebounds. Azura Stevens looked the most like herself since returning from injury. And Taylor again provided a burst off the bench, scoring 15 points on 6-for-13 shooting.</p><p>But without the ability to get stops, the Sky are missing what fueled their 3-1 start.</p><p>Cloud, for her part, still thinks the defense can turn around.</p><p>‘‘To me, defense is about pride, preparation, connectivity, our willingness to be there for one another, to be in gaps for the duration of the shot clock and then end the possession,’’ Cloud said. ‘‘If we get stops, we get to do what we want, which is run in transition, which we’re actually pretty good at.’’</p><p>Transition offense is another thing that has disappeared in this four-game skid. The Sky scored only four fast-break points against the Mystics.</p><p>There’s plenty of season left to turn things around. But the Sky first have to rediscover the veteran wisdom that was supposed to be their edge.</p>

entries.title: Cubs wary of May malaise ending with calendar flipped to June: ‘What are we going to do moving forward?’
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> might have put their recent 10-game losing streak and a miserable end to May behind them.</p><p>But the sting is still there.</p><p>It’s been a bizarre first two months for the Cubs, who rattled off two 10-game win streaks before plummeting out of first place with 10 straight defeats.</p><p>“Guys have been playing this game a long time in this locker room,” starting pitcher <b>Colin Rea</b> told the Sun-Times on Tuesday. “And you could probably go around the room and say that no one’s [experienced] the start to the season that we’ve had.”</p><p>There seemed to be a monkey-off-the-back moment when the Cubs stopped their slide with a couple wins last week in Pittsburgh. But a sour weekend series in St. Louis followed, and the Cubs finished May in a 5-16 rut. They’ve gone seven consecutive series without a series win.</p><p>And then they dropped the first of a 22-game stretch against teams that started the month below .500, a 2-1 loss to the Athletics on Tuesday night.</p><p>The championship-level expectations at Wrigley Field promised something much different than this.</p><p>“This has been a wake-up call, I hope, for everyone,” righty pitcher <b>Jameson Taillon</b> said after the game. “Nothing’s going to be handed to us. And the Brewers are for real again, they’re a very good team. Our division’s really good. The league’s really tough. And it’s going to take a lot of work to dig ourselves out of this.</p><p>“There’s urgency. Once you lose 10 in a row, I think the urgency’s at a pretty high level, to be honest.”</p><p>The Cubs only had one hit after the second inning Tuesday, with 20 of the final 22 hitters retired. They obviously have yet to exorcise what ailed them during the losing streak.</p><p>“When you’re winning all those games, you walk in the clubhouse and you expect to win that day,” Rea said. “It was rough there when we were losing. Guys were going through some rough patches, and some guys still are.</p><p>“After we won in Pittsburgh, my thoughts were: ‘Let’s see what happens the next couple weeks.’ Because it was just two games. ‘Yeah, it feels nice to put the losing streak behind us, but what are we going to do moving forward after we win a couple?’”</p><p>So far, it hasn’t been much prettier than it was during the skid. It’s time for the Cubs to get things right before it gets too late.</p><p>“There’s still a lot of time left. But you don’t want to fall into a trap of getting too comfortable when stuff isn’t going very well,” center fielder <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> said. “There comes a time when you do want to turn it around and it kind of has to [turn around].</p><p>“A ‘wake-up call’ is a nice way to put it.”</p><p><b>PCA thriving at the top</b></p><p>Since manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> shook up his lineup and moved Crow-Armstrong to the top, things have been going well for the All Star.</p><p>In 10 games batting in the Nos. 1 and 2 spots in the lineup, he’s hitting .308/.404/.462.</p><p>“I’m very confident in my work right now,” Crow-Armstrong said. “I’ve seen it pay some nice dividends, but I’m just confident because of the work and the plan I take into each at-bat.”</p><p>“I told him this: ‘There’s a responsibility of hitting first in the lineup. We are choosing you to hit most,’” Counsell said. “That’s a responsibility. Hopefully that means something.”</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-c90005" name="list-c90005"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, pageNumber=1, titleUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs, inverseColors=false, items=[{type=Image, publishDate=June 02, 2026 06:57 PM, categoryUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs, anchorId=promo-350000, category=[{items=[Cubs]}], description=[{items=[The Cubs will get two of their better starting pitchers back soon. entries.title: ICE agents shock man with Taser, barrel into car during chaotic arrest in Albany Park
entries.summary: <p>Federal agents chased and detained a man Tuesday morning in Albany Park, crashing into a woman's car during the pursuit and threatening residents who gathered at a chaotic scene.</p><p>A Sun-Times reporter witnessed the scene and its aftermath.</p><p>The arrest comes amid a continued effort by federal immigration authorities to carry out arrests in the Chicago area, months after the end of Operation Midway Blitz — the Trump administration's pummeling deportation campaign that led to thousands of arrests.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/ysQNeEB3ecE?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="ICE agents shock man with Taser, barrel into car during chaotic arrest in Albany Park"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>From the start of this year through mid-March, 580 <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/immigration/2026/05/07/rapid-responders-immigration-enforcement-ice-puno-mimi-guiracoch-pilsen-unidos-nuestro-orgullo-casa-dupage-workers-center" target="_blank" >people have been detained in the Chicago area</a><u>,</u> according to a Sun-Times/WBEZ analysis of data from the Deportation Data Project.</p><p>Tuesday's incident started at 8:07 a.m., when a black Nissan SUV carrying one agent turned east onto Lawrence Avenue from Kedzie Avenue, chasing a shirtless man. A second black Nissan SUV carrying more agents then pulled out of a nearby parking lot and hit a woman’s car in an apparent effort to block the man from running.</p><p>The agents were wearing Department of Homeland Security badges and patches associated with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.</p><p>Three agents ultimately wrestled the man to the ground as he screamed for help, asking agents to get off him as he was held under the front bumper of one of the SUVs. One agent then shocked him with a Taser.</p><p>The agent also aimed the weapon at bystanders and a journalist. Another agent pulled out a can of pepper spray and pointed it at the crowd as he waved away passing vehicles.</p><p>During the scuffle, an agent dropped a fully loaded bullet magazine onto the street. entries.title: 9 arrested during teen takeover in Naperville, officials say
entries.summary: <p>Nine people, including five minors, were arrested during a large gathering of teens Monday night in Naperville, police said.</p><p>Large groups began to gather downtown Naperville around 5 p.m., according to Naperville police. Several teams of officers worked the gathering, during which "several juveniles and young adults chose to commit violations of state law and local ordinances," Naperville police said in a enws release.</p><p>The crowds were dispersed by 11 p.m. By the end of the gathering, Naperville police issued nearly three dozen citations alongside the arrests, police said.</p><p>No injuries were reported. Large teen gatherings, commonly known as teen takeovers, in Chicago have sometimes turned violent, leaving city leaders, parents and anti-violence advocates worried about the trend, where word of the gatherings often spreads online.</p><p>"We’ve been very clear on our stance. We want people to come to our city, patronize our businesses, and enjoy all the amenities Naperville has to offer," Naperville Police Chief Jason Arres said in the release. "But if you break the law, there will be no warnings; there will be no second chances. We’ve tried that approach, and it was met with a lot of disrespect and lawlessness. So, as last night proved, we will not hesitate to make arrests and issue citations for breaking the law."</p><p>A 15-year-old boy from Bolingbrook was arrested for obstructing idenfitication, Naperville police said.</p><p>Four 17-year-old boys were arrested, police said. One of them, from Plainfield, was arrested for battery. Another boy from Bolingbrook was arrested for battery, assault and illegal possession of cannabis and tobacco by a minor. Another 17-year-old from Romeoville was arrested for disobeying a peace officer, and one from Aurora was arrested for obstructing identification and criminal trespass to state supported land</p><p>Sudais Oyekanmi, an 18-year-old from Aurora, was arrested for obstructing identification. Marshun Smith and Tyler Sims, both 18 from Romeoville, also were arrested. Smith faces charges of attempted aggravated assault on a peace officer and Sims faces charges of battery and obstructing a peace officer.<br></p>

entries.title: Why does Chicago use Comic Sans on some elevator inspection certificates?
entries.summary: <p>Have you ever ridden a Chicago elevator that groaned a little too loud or jerked a little too hard? Maybe to reassure yourself, you looked at the inspection certificate, but what you found was even more concerning: not the inspection date, but the font of just a few words on the document.</p><p>The line in question is toward the top left corner of the page. It reads, “This certifies that, I have, [ON THIS DATE] inspected the elevator at [ADDRESS].”</p><p>The words “this certifies that” are in Comic Sans. Yes, the font used for lemonade stands is used on an official city document. But Comic Sans doesn’t appear on every inspection certificate.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a </div> </div><p>Why would the city of Chicago use what’s arguably the most unserious font for a serious document? And why just three words?</p><p>Designers may choose a font to convey a certain tone to their readers. But in this case, it may offer a peek into the technological backend of local government. It might also be an indicator for requesting an elevator inspection.</p><h3>What’s the big deal with Comic Sans?</h3><p>If a font itself could be a meme, Comic Sans would be it. More often than not, it’s used to convey sarcasm. So why would the city use it on an official document?</p><p>Comic Sans didn’t always carry this reputation. In 1994, Microsoft wanted a new font for its desktop program called Microsoft Bob. According to company designer Vincent Connare, the font they were initially using, Times New Roman, did not match the relaxed vibe they were going for.</p><p>Drawing on inspiration from comic books, Connare designed Comic Sans to feel friendly, casual and easygoing.</p><p>As home computers grew in popularity throughout the 1990s, Comic Sans and other design tools became more accessible.</p><p>“ This typeface being widely available to the public was one of the reasons why it got so widely adopted,” said Lee Zelenak, designer and lecturer at the DePaul University School of Design. “ But when you have this democratization of design and everyone can be a designer, you lose a little bit of that control over what they're gonna use it for.”</p><div class="Enhancement" prank? According to the city’s Department of Buildings, which oversees all things elevators, including inspecting and issuing certificates, no.</p><p>The agency said elevator inspection certificates are all system-generated. Whatever is causing the font to change is happening on the technological backend, which means the city’s central IT department has the answer.</p><p>It appears the quirky font choice happened when the city migrated old software to different servers, according to Grant Ulrich, managing deputy commissioner at the Department of Buildings.</p><p>“If the font is not installed with this really old software, it picks the font with the next alphabetical name in the list of whatever fonts are available on that server,” Ulrich said. “So this was not a choice. From the Daley era to the current administration, the fonts go from Blackletter to Corsiva, then Comic Sans and then Segoe Script, respectively — skipping over a number of options in between.</p><p>As for the fact that it’s only three words, “This certifies that,” with a different font than the rest of the document?</p><p>Ulrich said that’s most likely attributed to a former city employee who is no longer around. (Typical workplace move, to blame a predecessor for the status quo.)</p><p>So if Comic Sans signals an inspection from the previous mayoral administration, should that be a concern? The Department of Buildings said no; it could simply mean the landlord or property manager may not have physically updated the certificate.</p><p>However, the elevator may still be due for an inspection. For that, call 311 or submit a service request <a class="Link" href="https://311.chicago.gov/s/service-request" target="_blank" >online</a>.</p><p>The Comic Sans certificates are still out there in elevators all across the city, but those quirky fonts may soon be a thing of the past. class="Figure-content"><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Emma Nippe</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><b>Emma Nippe</b> is an economist living in Albany Park. She is a self-described architecture and design nerd, which is one of the reasons why she loves living in Chicago. She couldn’t help but wonder why a city known for its skyscrapers, aka buildings that need elevators, would have such poorly designed inspection certificates.<br><br>Emma first started noticing these certificates after traveling a lot for work. She often found herself in non-luxurious, design oriented cities. But they still have well-formatted certificates.<br><br>“ And these places have elevator inspection certificates that are top of the line, like graphic design minded, all single font, beautiful serif,” she said. “ To come back to Chicago, a city again, known for its architecture and its design, that no one has noticed this…. It’s just baffling to me.”<br><br><b>Harrison Pious</b> is a salesperson living in Logan Square. He is, generally speaking, not a fan of elevators, so he often checks the elevator certificates for inspection dates. Once he noticed the Comic Sans on the certificate, he saw it everywhere.<br><br>Harrison appreciates that he wasn’t the only person who noticed this.<br><br> ”It makes me feel far less crazy that I wasn’t the only person both noticing and bothered by it,” he said.<br><br>Over time, though, the font has grown on him. And he may miss it when it’s gone. “I’ve also kind of grown to like it, in a really perverse way,” he said. “It’s something so quirky in Chicago that, of course we would have something like this.”</div> </div><p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-750000" name="html-embed-module-750000"></a><script async src="https://modules.wearehearken.com/wbez/embed/4190.js"></script> </div> </div><p></p>

involved former Mayor Lori Lightfoot's "previous mayoral administration." But two high level aides to Johnson had ties to EKI-Digital, the consulting company central to the scandal.</p><p><b>John Roberson</b>: One aide, John Roberson, was involved in the decision to pay EKI $600,000 in taxpayer money despite red flags about some of its municipal work. Roberson was Johnson’s chief operating officer from about the time Johnson took office in May 2023 until July 2025, when he left to work for the Obama Foundation. Roberson was "managing principal" for EKI in 2014 and 2015, according to his LinkedIn profile.</p><p><b>Michael Belsky</b>: Johnson’s current City Hall comptroller, Michael Belsky, worked for EKI when its deal was forged with Lightfoot top aide Paul W. Goodrich, and Goodrich’s son landed a paid internship with EKI. </div> </div><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whikthk-l-ty/" target="_blank" >Chef Zubair Mohajir is having fun going into business with friends</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whikthk-l-tj/" target="_blank" >Ximena N. Beltran Quan Kiu</a></h5><p>Getting laid off tends to be a stressful experience for the majority of people. However, for chef Zubair Mohajir — a multiple James Beard Award nominee, "Chopped" winner and "Top Chef" contender — it became the day his life began.</p><p>"I was so freaking happy," said Mohajir, 41, of his banking stint that ended in 2008. “But then I had to figure out what I do for work.”</p><p>Today, Mohajir is the chef and owner of the Michelin Guide-recognized Coach House, Lilac Tiger, Mirra and Sarima Cafe. He is opening three new concepts this year to add to his growing empire.</p><p>Mariela in the Loop, "a coastal restaurant based in nostalgia," opened last month. Muhājir — "the translation of it in Urdu, in Arabic, means 'migrant" — in Lincoln Park is an extension of the Coach House that will debut in the summer. And Bobo, "a really vibrant bar where people feel like they’re stepping through a wildly disorienting 'Doctor Strange'-like portal into the Manila night," will be tucked away behind Muhājir.</p><p>The hospitality concepts Mohajir owns with several different partners do not operate under a parent company. That might change one day, but for now, Mohajir says he’s just having fun going into business with friends.</p><p>"I really love opening restaurants," Mohajir said. "The best calls I like to make are to friends saying, 'Hey, quit your job, move back. Let’s open a restaurant.' You attack the world differently when you’re walking in step with somebody."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whikthk-l-tt/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>Where can you find the best bagels in Chicago? What makes them the best?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Respond via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). We may run your answer in a future newsletter or story.</i></p><p>Yesterday, we asked you: <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whikthk-l-ti/" target="_blank" >What’s a song you feel perfectly captures the Chicago Blues sound?</a></p><p>Here’s some of what you said…</p><p>"'Messin’ with the Kid' by Buddy Guy and Junior Wells always just said 'Chicago blues' to me." — <i>Brad Wilson</i></p><p>"'55th Street Boogie' by Hound Dog Taylor. It captures the energy of the city — nobody is crying in their beer in this song." — <i>Jeff Varda</i></p><p>"'Blue and Lonesome' by Little Walter, because it is electric blues with a solid bond to the roots due to the harmonica sound. The lyrics express the sense of loneliness in a big city after the Great Migration from the South. Even the life and death of Little Walter is the personification of the blues." — <i>Giovanni Taverna</i></p><p>"'Sweet Home Chicago' by Robert Johnson. It’s the unofficial soundtrack of the city. Everyone knows it, everyone sings along, and it captures the pride, energy and soul of Chicago. Pair it with a Chicago-style hot dog and you’ve got the full Chicago experience." — <i>Courtney Cager</i></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Eydie Cubarrubia</p><hr><p><i>The Chicago Sun-Times is a nonprofit supported by readers like you. entries.title: Illinois Comptroller Susana Mendoza announces campaign for Chicago mayor
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Comptroller Susana Mendoza announced Wednesday she'll be running for mayor of Chicago in next year's election. </p><p>Mendoza made the announcement in a<a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UU6kW1W6wDM" target="_blank" > YouTube video post. </a></p><p>Since Mayor Brandon Johnson took office in 2023, Mendoza has telegraphed her mayoral ambitions with a steady stream of social media statements criticizing many of his progressive policies, while positioning herself as a centrist, pro-police Democrat.</p><p>She took passing shots at Johnson for his handling of public safety, Chicago Public Schools and mass transit, but lit him up for a lack of “economic growth” under his watch, according to Mendoza.</p><p>Mendoza has spent three terms as Illinois comptroller and announced she wouldn’t be seeking a fourth term last July.</p><p>In 2019, Mendoza finished fifth on the ballet, garnering nine percent of votes in the general election before Lori Lightfoot defeated Toni Preckwinkle in a runoff election. <br></p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams' 'Madden 27' cover revealed
entries.summary: <p>It’s official: Caleb Williams is the face of Madden 27.</p><p>The quarterback became the first <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> player to ever grace the front of the main edition of the video game Wednesday morning when EA Sports announced him as their choice. They released two covers. On the standard edition of the video game, Williams is pictured throwing a jump pass. On the deluxe edition, Williams is shown rubbing his biceps, the celebration he used that matched his “Iceman” nickname.</p><p>The video game will be released Aug. 13.</p><p>The Bears won their first playoff game in 15 years last season with Williams under center, but it was the way that he did it that captivated the country, leading the Bears to six comeback victories. His heave to tight end Cole Kmet to tie the Rams in the final seconds of a playoff game was perhaps his most memorable play of the season — though his game-winning throw against the Packers to DJ Moore was named the league’s Moment of the Year. Williams’ jump throw is reminiscent of his playoff pass to receiver Rome Odunze.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">The jump. The <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/Madden27?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#Madden27</a> Cover. The future. <br><br>Gridiron heroics earn <a href="https://x.com/CALEBcsw?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@CALEBcsw</a> Cover Athlete status! <br><br>Full reveal Thursday, 6/4 at 8 PM ET<br>🔗: <a href="https://t.co/REHXoqeZIf">https://t.co/REHXoqeZIf</a> <a href="https://t.co/VBzO40XbdF">pic.twitter.com/VBzO40XbdF</a></p>— Madden NFL 26 (@EAMaddenNFL) <a href="https://x.com/EAMaddenNFL/status/2062141869019054323?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">June 3, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>In a statement, Williams said that finding out that he was the cover choice “was like my childhood dream was coming true.” He grew up playing the game and called it a “full-circle moment.”</p><p>EA Sports vice president of franchise strategy and marketing Evan Dexter called him the Bears’ “electric, generational quarterback.”</p><p>Images of Williams on the cover <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/05/31/bears-caleb-williams-madden-cover-speculation-quarterback-nfl-video-game" target="_blank" >leaked on social media over the weekend</a>. An EA Sports event scheduled Thursday in Chicago further tipped off his inclusion.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">behind the scenes of <a href="https://x.com/CALEBcsw?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@CALEBcsw</a>’s <a href="https://x.com/EAMaddenNFL?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@EAMaddenNFL</a> cover 🎬 <a href="https://t.co/3D8poZSQiB">pic.twitter.com/3D8poZSQiB</a></p>— NFL (@NFL) <a href="https://x.com/NFL/status/2062143415567999398?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">June 3, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>No Bears player had ever appeared on the cover of the video game, though former Bears center Roberto Garza was on the Spanish-language cover in 2009. Super Bowl-winning Eagles running back Saquon Barkley was on the cover last year, with Bills quarterback Josh Allen and 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey the two years before.<br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Mother regrets choices that impacted daughters' lives
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I was in an abusive relationship for 15 years that affected my children badly. I have had emotional problems since I was a child, which caused me to stay in the relationship long past the point I should have left.</p><p>My two daughters left home at 16 and 13 to live with their fathers. Both of their fathers allowed the girls to smoke and consume alcohol and drugs. I was still trying to wrap my head around my abusive relationship, which I stayed in for about eight years on and off after my youngest left. It affected my emotional state, and the abuse worsened.</p><p>Both of my daughters quit school and had children young. Their lives and potential were ruined, and they still struggle. They were fragile birds who suffered broken wings as a result of my relationship, and I can't forgive myself.</p><p>Although I finally left for good, they still don't let me be their mother in a way I should be. Every day I suffer emotionally because of the state of all our lives, and I'm really hurting inside. I don't think these feelings will ever go away or subside. Please help me. — <i>DYING INSIDE IN NEW ENGLAND</i></p><p><b>DEAR DYING:</b> Before you can help your daughters, you are going to have to help yourself. A way to begin would be to reach out to the National Domestic Violence Hotline (thehotline.org), which offers counseling for abused spouses. It offers local resources in every state.</p><p>In order for your daughters to heal themselves, they will first have to admit they, too, need help. While it may be too late for you to "mother" your daughters in the way you would like, there may be help for them if they are willing to admit they need it. The National Domestic Violence Hotline can tell them where to find it when they're ready.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Our niece became acquainted with a man through a website. They have been "dating" for more than four years now. Here is the thing: He refuses to be introduced. With one exception, none of her family or friends has met her boyfriend.</p><p>My wife and I have invited them to our home, but they have turned down all offers. He has conveniently been elsewhere at family events, such as her child's wedding, birthday parties and holiday meals. Oddly, she has met his family and keeps up with them on social media.</p><p>I have discussed this with others in the family and have been told by some that "it's her life." (No argument there.) I respect their privacy, but if her family has meaning to either of them, shouldn't we meet him? — <i>IGNORED UNCLE IN TENNESSEE</i></p><p><b>DEAR UNCLE:</b> It does seem odd that with "one exception" no one in the family has met your niece's boyfriend. Because this is so concerning to you, perhaps you should pick up a phone and discuss this with her. Is there something that she is hiding, such as cultural or religious differences? Is there an age disparity? Could the gentleman be incarcerated? There is always a reason. You won't know unless you ask.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>For an excellent guide to becoming a better conversationalist and a more sociable person, order "How to Be Popular." Send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby, Popularity Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: USAID cuts have a hand in Ebola outbreak overseas
entries.summary: <p>The Ebola <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/world/africa/40-dead-ebola-outbreak-dr-congo-uganda-rcna347745" target="_blank" >outbreak</a> currently devastating the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda didn't come out of thin air. It grew from the vacuum left behind by deliberate policy decisions made here in the United States.</p><p>This is the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wsj.com/world/africa/ebola-outbreak-explained-4ab4414f" target="_blank" >third largest Ebola</a> outbreak in recorded history. As of late May, there were over <a class="Link" href="https://www.infectioncontroltoday.com/view/defunded-exposed-how-u-s-aid-cuts-broken-trust-fueled-2026-ebola-crisis" target="_blank" >900 suspected cases</a> in the Congo alone. The strain spreading through the region has no vaccine or targeted treatment. But the main difference between previous Ebola outbreaks and this one is that the systems that were supposed to catch and contain them early have been <a class="Link" href="https://spacedaily.com/d-the-third-largest-ebola-outbreak-on-record-is-spreading-through-drc-and-uganda-and-aid-workers-former-usaid-officials-and-global-health-experts-say-recent-us-funding-cuts-have-made-detecti/ " target="_blank" >defunded.</a></p><p>The U.S. Agency for International Development sent approximately <a class="Link" href="https://spacedaily.com/d-the-third-largest-ebola-outbreak-on-record-is-spreading-through-drc-and-uganda-and-aid-workers-former-usaid-officials-and-global-health-experts-say-recent-us-funding-cuts-have-made-detecti/" target="_blank" >$1.2 billion</a> in foreign aid to the Congo in 2024. By the final three months of 2025, that figure had collapsed to just <a class="Link" href="https://spacedaily.com/d-the-third-largest-ebola-outbreak-on-record-is-spreading-through-drc-and-uganda-and-aid-workers-former-usaid-officials-and-global-health-experts-say-recent-us-funding-cuts-have-made-detecti/" target="_blank" >$67 million</a>. While that $1.2 billion figure may sound large at face value, USAID represented only <a class="Link" href="https://usafacts.org/explainers/what-does-the-us-government-do/agency/us-agency-for-international-development/" target="_blank" >0.3% of the federal budget</a>, compared to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.usaspending.gov/agency/department-of-defense?fy=2026" target="_blank" >Department of Defense’s 13%</a>. </p><p>Many workers with experience responding to Ebola outbreaks, and critically, the relationships they’d built with local health officials, were fired when USAID was dismantled. As one former USAID official put it, the agency served as <a class="Link" href="https://abc17news.com/news/national-world/cnn-world/2026/05/21/us-funding-cuts-have-hampered-response-to-the-deadly-ebola-crisis-aid-workers-say/" target="_blank" >“the glue” coordinating</a> health officials, NGOs and donors. Additionally, <a class="Link" href="https://www.ms.now/news/ebola-outbreak-trump-usaid-cuts-congo" target="_blank" >Kathleen Borgueta</a>, who managed the East Africa portfolio for USAID’s global health bureau until 2025, said, “The backbone of our workforce and our ability to respond just isn't there anymore."</p><p>The human cost of these decisions is staggering, and it extends far beyond this outbreak. A recent <a class="Link" href="https://www.thelancet.com/journals/langlo/article/PIIS2214-109X(26)00008-2/fulltext" target="_blank" >peer-reviewed study</a> by the Barcelona Institute for Global Health projects that <a class="Link" href="https://www.thelancet.com/article/S0140-6736(25)01186-9/fulltext" target="_blank" >global aid cuts</a> could lead to at least 9.4 million additional deaths by 2030 — including 2.5 million children under 5 — if current funding trends continue. Even before this Ebola crisis, <a class="Link" href="https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/chikungunya/quick-takes-death-toll-usaid-cuts-withdrawal-chikungunya-vaccine-funding-updated-ebola" target="_blank" >760,000 people</a> had already died as a result of these cuts as of January.</p><p>Viruses don’t care about ideology or borders. When we dismantle the systems that detect and contain them abroad, we don’t save money. We defer costs in lives. Americans must ask their elected representatives: Who is accountable?</p><p><i>Ezekiel Wilson-Porter, Skokie</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-600000" name="module-600000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Anti-Muslim hate often goes unchecked </h3><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/05/20/nx-s1-5827053/san-diego-mosque-shooting-victims" target="_blank" >deadly San Diego mosque shooting</a> driven by anti-Muslim hate doesn't surprise me. It proves once more that words have consequences. For American Muslims who are on the receiving end of <a class="Link" href="https://religionnews.com/2026/05/26/the-anti-muslim-rhetoric-that-inspired-teen-gunmen-has-been-increasing-for-years/" target="_blank" >rising Islamophobia</a>, the barbs are thorns that pierce deeply. But many in the non-Muslim world and some mainstream media journalists mostly ignore or brush off this vile, verbal abuse.</p><p>When U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., calls Muslims the enemy <a class="Link" href="https://aldailynews.com/tubervilles-anti-muslim-rhetoric-catches-on-among-alabama-republicans-in-campaign-year/" target="_blank" >“inside the gates,”</a> U.S. Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., says he <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/02/17/randy-fine-muslims-dogs-resign/" target="_blank" >prefers dogs over Muslims</a> and far-right political activist Laura Loomer — who has President Donald Trump's ear — says Muslims should be deported and are an <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/20/us/san-diego-islamophobia-violence.html" target="_blank" >“invasive species,” </a>why should it be a surprise that the two teenage gunmen learned to hate Muslims?</p><p>Such odious quotes are hate speech masquerading as free speech. Many Americans know the use of the N-word is unacceptable and are quick to call out antisemitism. But they don't react the same way when it comes to anti-Muslim hate, and in many cases, are OK with it. </p><p>It is sad that Republican leaders have proposed the Preserving a Sharia-Free America <a class="Link" href="https://www.govtrack.us/congress/bills/119/hr5722" target="_blank" >Act</a> instead of addressing the rising hate toward Muslims within their ranks. </p><p>The pending legislation states: “Any alien in the United States found to be an adherent of Sharia law by the Secretary of State, Secretary of Homeland Security, or Attorney General shall have any immigration benefit, immigration relief, or visa revoked, be considered inadmissible or deportable, and shall be removed from the United States.” </p><p>That would make every Muslim who prays, fasts or goes to Hajj vulnerable.</p><p>U.S. Rep. Pramila Jayapal's, D-Wash., description of a congressional hearing on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/04/13/sharia-meaning-muslims-similarities-united-states-constitution-salam-al-marayati" >“Sharia law”</a> as "bizarre" was a bit mild. But she rightly criticized Republican lawmakers for unfairly targeting every mosque as a <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DYXzOrrMFUT/" target="_blank" >“beachhead of terrorism.”</a></p><p>It is important to note that it's not just the racist politicians maligning Muslims. Some journalists have been reckless with their words and selection of stories and commentary, often aligning terrorism with Islam and Muslims. </p><p>I suggest media workers and politicians take a crash course in anti-Muslim hate and relearn how ignorance and hate speech can lead to prejudice, stereotyping, reductionism and physical attacks. On every March 15 — the United Nations-designated <a class="Link" href="https://www.un.org/en/observances/anti-islamophobia-day" target="_blank" >“International Day to Combat Islamophobia”</a> — media representatives should take a pledge to not use words and phrases that are overtly or covertly Islamophobic and to cover our communities fairly. </p><p>If nothing changes, we American Muslims can only ask, “What comes next?”</p><p><i>Dr. Javeed Akhter, Oak Brook</i></p><h3>Trump’s bad deals</h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/116630919376298273" target="_blank" >“I don’t make bad deals!”</a> President Donald Trump recently posted on Truth Social. </p><p>Hmmm. <a class="Link" href="https://abcnews.com/US/trumps-taj-mahal-casino-8th-world-closure-years/story?id=42762369" target="_blank" >Trump Taj Mahal</a>. <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2021/02/17/968656595/in-seconds-atlantic-citys-trump-plaza-and-casino-is-reduced-to-rubble" target="_blank" >Trump Plaza Hotel and Casino</a>. <a class="Link" href="https://www.abi.org/feed-item/trump-entertainment-resorts-files-for-chapter-11-bankruptcy-protection-in-delaware" target="_blank" >Trump Entertainment Resorts</a>. <a class="Link" href="https://www.thetakeout.com/1901963/why-trump-steaks-failed/" target="_blank" >Trump Steaks</a>. <a class="Link" href="https://www.bloomberg.com/features/2016-trump-vodka/?embedded-checkout=true" target="_blank" >Trump Vodka</a>. <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/do-trump-products-really-thrive" target="_blank" >Trump Ice bottled water</a>. <a class="Link" href="https://slate.com/business/2016/03/the-lesson-of-donald-trump-s-failed-sketchy-mortgage-business.html" target="_blank" >Trump Mortgage</a>. <a class="Link" href="https://www.rollingstone.com/politics/politics-lists/the-many-business-failures-of-donald-trump-12488/" target="_blank" >GoTrump.com</a>. <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/04/30/us/trump-shuttle-budget-carriers" target="_blank" >Trump Shuttle</a>. <a class="Link" href="https://www.vox.com/2015/8/19/9176285/donald-trump-board-game" target="_blank" >Trump: The Game</a>. <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/magazine/story/2016/08/donald-trump-magazine-employee-confessional-bankrupt-2016-214155/" target="_blank" >Trump magazine</a>. <a class="Link" href="https://abcnews.com/US/judge-finalizes-25-million-settlement-victims-donald-trumps/story?id=54347237" target="_blank" >Trump University</a>.</p><p>I think Trump is spot on. He doesn't make bad deals. He makes horrific ones.</p><p><i>Wes Dickson, Orland Park</i></p><h3>Trump is worth a penny at best </h3><p>I fully agree with having our current president's likeness on currency. <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/05/30/edith-pritchett-cartoon-trump-250-bill-proposal/" target="_blank" >But a $250 bill</a> is not the best option. I say the penny, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2025/12/17/end-penny-us-mint-production-chicago-businesses-coin-shortage" >now no longer in produc</a>tion, would have been ideal. </p><p><i>Todd Miglieri, Evergreen Park</i></p><h3>Poking the Bears </h3><p>Thank you, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/06/01/pritzker-bears-indiana-illinois-stadium-bill" target="_blank" >Illinois House, </a>for standing up to the Bears!</p><p><i>Warren Rodgers Jr., Orland Park</i></p><h3>Buh-bye!</h3><p>To paraphrase the famous Gerald Ford-related front-page New York Daily News <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2006/12/28/nyregion/28veto.html" target="_blank" >headline</a>: Illinois to the McCaskeys: Drop dead!</p><p><i>Dennis Allen, Wilmette</i><br></p>

entries.title: ‘Takeover’ label unhelpful to teens not looking for trouble
entries.summary: <p>In May 2022, 16-year-old <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2022/5/16/23074890/seandell-holliday-bean-shooting-millennium-park" >Seandell Holliday</a> was shot and killed near the Bean during a large youth gathering at Millennium Park. It was a tragedy — and it set the terms for nearly every conversation Chicago has had about teen gatherings since. More police. Earlier curfews. Restricted park access. </p><p>The question driving every proposal: How do we prevent this from happening again?</p><p>That is a reasonable question, but it is not the only one. Four years later, with gatherings continuing to grow, it may not even be the most important.</p><p>I <a class="Link" href="https://osf.io/preprints/socarxiv/3wazu_v1" target="_blank" >study</a> these gatherings. The question I keep returning to is both simpler and harder: What is actually happening here, and what is it telling us?</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-090000" name="module-090000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>"Teen takeover" is not a neutral term. It tells you, before you've looked closely, that space is being seized, that something is being taken from someone to whom it rightfully belongs. It arrives with its verdict already built in.</p><p>What if showing up at Millennium Park — or the lakefront, or Downtown — is not a seizure of space but a claim on it? The kind of claim any young person makes when they go somewhere they belong, or believe they belong?</p><p>Decades of research on how media frames Black youth in public space are consistent: presence is coded as a threat, regardless of what is actually occurring. The language of "takeover" does not describe a social reality so much as it constructs one. Once that construction is in place, every subsequent decision — about resources, response and who deserves to be where — flows from it.</p><p>I am not suggesting there are no legitimate public safety concerns — there are. Some gatherings have escalated into violence, and that matters. But escalation is not the defining feature of most of what we call "teen takeovers," and treating it as such leads to responses calibrated to the exception rather than the norm.</p><h3>What Chicago may be watching</h3><h3></h3><p>Young people from the South Side are attending the same gatherings as those from the West Side. For anyone familiar with Chicago's social geography — the territorial divisions that have shaped neighborhood life, sometimes violently, for generations — that is not a small thing. </p><p>Those boundaries have historically been among the most consequential and dangerous in this city. The fact that they appear to be softening, with young people crossing them publicly and in groups, is remarkable.</p><p>When you follow someone across the city and develop a sense of connection, geography becomes less determinative — the gathering becomes a place to meet someone you already know, just not yet in person. These are not random crowds. They are networked communities finding physical space for existing digital ties.</p><p>What Chicago may be witnessing is not chaos. It may be a generation quietly redrawing some of its most entrenched and dangerous social maps.</p><p>Young people gather. They always have. What changes when the sanctioned places for that gathering disappear — the recreation centers that close, the programming that gets cut, the neighborhood spaces left behind while Downtown infrastructure is maintained — is not the impulse to gather. It is the location.</p><h3>Teens look for free, open space</h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://greatcities.uic.edu/news-stories/a-normalized-crisis-youth-and-young-adult-joblessness-and-disconnection-data-brief-feb-2026/" target="_blank" >Teen unemployment</a> in Chicago has remained a problem, leaving many young people with time and energy but few structured outlets. Downtown public space — free, open and accessible — becomes the default. The same visibility that makes these spaces appealing also turns the gathering into a news event.</p><p>The city disinvests in youth spaces. Youth find other spaces. The city responds with enforcement. That enforcement deepens distrust and escalates the very conflicts it was meant to prevent. Then the cycle repeats.</p><p>The challenge for city leaders is not just whether to allocate more resources for enforcement, but also to invest in programming, safe spaces, economic opportunities and fostering relationships between young people and trusted adults that address the underlying issues these gatherings reveal.</p><p>Teen takeovers are not a youth crime wave. They are a legible social signal: Young people, largely low-income and of color, navigating a city that has not invested in them, claiming visibility in spaces that belong to them as much as to anyone else. </p><p>If Chicago treats that as a crisis of disorder, it will keep reaching for tools that make things worse. If it treats it as information — about what this city owes its young people — it might finally build responses that could actually help.</p><p><i>Almethia C. Franklin, Ph.D., is a Chicago native and postdoctoral research associate at the Institute for Research on Race and Public Policy at the University of Illinois Chicago. She is also an assistant professor of criminal justice and sociology at Concordia University Chicago. She studies large-scale youth gatherings in Chicago and cities across the country.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-eb0000" name="module-eb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Honoring Juneteenth, Black Music at an unlikely place: Andrew Jackson's plantation
entries.summary: <p>This Juneteenth I will stand at the Hermitage and help celebrate Black music. The Hermitage was Andrew Jackson’s plantation outside Nashville. I want to be honest about how strange that is.</p><p>I am descended from slaves and from the men who owned and abused them. The men who denied them their God-given right to freedom. My family was enslaved by the Blands of Virginia. Richard Bland was the famous one. He was a patriot before there was a country. He told the king and Parliament that a shackle chafes a man no matter how well you polish it. His young cousin Thomas Jefferson asked him to bring a bill to make it easier to free the enslaved. Bland did it. He was denounced as an enemy of his country. Then he went home and kept his 30. He died still holding them.</p><p>That is my inheritance. My grandmother, Mamie Bland Todd, is the griot of our family. She carries 200 years of it. Her great-grandfather Frederick was the only enslaved man named in his owner’s will, and the will was written to protect him. The man who owned Frederick was his own brother. That is how close the blood runs. Thomas Jefferson is my cousin. He wrote that all men are created equal. Robert E. Lee is my cousin too. He took up arms to keep my other ancestors in chains. I carry the blood of the man who argued for freedom and the blood of those he would not free. I resent his cruelty. I pray my children show his courage against the men who would be kings. That is the duality of this nation.</p><p>So I know something about awkward ground.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fc0000" name="module-fc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>The Hermitage is beautiful. A thousand acres. A white mansion. Gardens. The tombs of the seventh president and his wife. It is also a graveyard. More than 300 men, women and children were enslaved there. Archaeologists are still finding their graves. The land was Native land first. He signed the Indian Removal Act. He set the Trail of Tears in motion. Settlers’ bones are in that ground. The bones of the enslaved. The ground is sacred for what is buried in it. It is stained for the same reason.</p><p>And we are going to sing on it.</p><p>Jackson owned the people there. He fathered no children, white or Black. Betty cooked for him, as her mother had before her. Her son Alfred was born on that land and lived there longer than any man. After freedom came he stayed. They put “Faithful Servant” on his stone. But once a white man told him slavery had its comforts, and Alfred asked him, “How would you like to be a slave?” The man had no answer.</p><p>For a while that felt like trespass. Who brings a celebration into a wound? Black music was not made in spite of that ground. It was made on it. The field holler. The spiritual. The work song that timed a hoe. People who were called property made them, and the songs said they were not. “Follow the Drinking Gourd” was a map to freedom. They sang it where the men who owned them could hear.</p><p>Juneteenth is the right day for it. Freedom came late, two and a half years after it was declared, to people who had been free in the eyes of God the whole time. The day does not pretend the delay away. It celebrates anyway.</p><p>So I will go. I will stand where Jackson stood and where the people he enslaved stood. I will not soften either truth. I will say their names if they let me.</p><p>We are more curious now than ever about how we are joined. I have a cousin who descends from the people who owned mine. We are kin. The country is like that.</p><p>Nothing feeds the American need for unity and hope like the music made by enslaved people and their children. It is the truest thing this country has made. And we are still singing it.</p><p>So this Juneteenth, on sacred and stained ground, we will sing. And we will remember the oldest truth Mamie Bland Todd ever taught me: our people were always free.</p><p>And — oddly, ironically, and even somewhat poetically — it happens to be the same lesson her own slaveholding forebear, Richard, helped teach both his young cousin Thomas and King George.</p><p>Freedom is inherent. It belongs to us from the beginning.</p><p><i>Ben Jealous is a professor of practice at the University of Pennsylvania and former president and CEO of the NAACP.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bc0000" name="module-bc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

</u></a>on $48-per-dozen artisanal bagels (in PopUp’s case) as the next frontier for expansion.</p><p>The nascent chain’s arrival in Chicago comes amid a nationwide premium bagel boom, driven partly by the dominance of breakfast (<a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/food-drink/2025/04/30/del-sur-bakery-chicago-lines" target="_blank" ><u>see flavormaxxing pastries</u></a>) as consumers pinch pennies elsewhere in their dining budgets. The wave of big money-backed newcomers follows a recent, citywide proliferation of indie bagel shops, whose artisanal products have sought to upend the longheld perception that Chicago just isn’t a bagel town.</p><p>As Big Bagel eyes aggressive expansion here, this fiercely independent food city is starting to push back. Is this town — and its clearly growing bagel appetite — big enough for all of them?</p><hr><p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-550000" name="html-embed-module-550000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-map" data-src="visualisation/29181806"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/29181806/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="map visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><hr><p>“We’re seeing it around the country, this bagel craze,” said Chris Hadermann, PopUp’s Chicago franchisee who is mostly Atlanta-based. “Heck, I’m all for it. I could argue that by having more options, it helps drive the standard for bagels even higher.”</p><p>It’s not just Big Bagel’s moment. Recent years have brought a flurry of homegrown indie bagel shops here, from actual pop-ups like Middle Brow’s comically charred, sourdough Beachwater Bagels each Saturday to seven-month-old Dorothy’s Bakery, serving up overnight fermented sourdough bagel sandwiches a 10-minute walk east of Hadermann’s inaugural Chicago site.</p><p>There are other locals, too. In Pilsen, Rosca proffers sourdough bagels made from freshly milled wheat berries that it infuses with Mexican-inspired flavors like red mole. South Loop-based Tilly Bagel Shop bakes fluffy, chewy sourdough bagels throughout the morning in two locations. Upmarket delicatessen Zeitlin’s recently added a second Lincoln Park location where it serves pert, springy bagel sandwiches. And if you are fast enough to get your order in at an unspecified time each Tuesday (tip: sign up for the text message service), Holey Dough & Co. will reward you with plump and squishy New York-style The investment fund Stripes invested $8 million in 2023, just after Goldberg opened his first brick-and-mortar shop in Manhattan. Since the fund became the majority owner of PopUp with an additional $27 million injection in 2024, PopUp has added 33 locations.</p><p>PopUp isn’t the only deep-pocketed newcomer sizing up the Chicago market. An outpost of New York icon H&H opened last year in Fulton Market<b>,</b> a decade after former Wall Street investor Jay Rushin bought the company with national expansion goals. D.C.-based deli Call Your Mother also brought its New York/Montreal-hybrid bagels to Bucktown<b> </b>this spring, after asset management fund Invus bought a majority stake.</p><p>Its location, around the corner from kettle-boiled indie stalwart BroBagel, drew the <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reels/DYjie-5oVhe/" target="_blank" ><u>ire</u></a> of the latter’s cofounder Bill Jacobs, who with his brothers owns Piece Pizzeria and Brewery. By then, commenters on <a class="Link" href="https://www.reddit.com/r/chicagofood/comments/1szylsd/has_popup_bagel_lost_their_damn_minds/" target="_blank" ><u>Reddit</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.tiktok.com/@bychrisvazquez/video/7632377404345896223" target="_blank" ><u>TikTok</u></a> were already taking issue with the prices and “morally questionable” consequences of supporting Big Bagel. Mindy’s Bakery owner Mindy Segal begged to differ, <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reel/DY4qmChuOwr/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsh=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==" target="_blank" ><u>arguing</u></a> that wherever consumers shop, they’re also “helping give salaries to hourly employees” just trying to pay their bills.</p><p>“We landed on Chicago because it’s a great food town and a large, dense area,” said PopUp’s Hadermann, also the co-founder, managing partner and CEO of Southern Proper Hospitality Group. “The amount of outreach from fans was also very, very exciting. The group out of New York kept me posted on inquiries about how badly Chicago needed a new bagel option.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-6f0000" name="image-6f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9a606cb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6488x3641+0+342/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F48%2F6d%2F1cbe0f604651b8583543b5c607d8%2Fbagels-260603-8.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7399a9e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6488x3641+0+342/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F48%2F6d%2F1cbe0f604651b8583543b5c607d8%2Fbagels-260603-8.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/949f19b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6488x3641+0+342/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F48%2F6d%2F1cbe0f604651b8583543b5c607d8%2Fbagels-260603-8.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Dozens of customers line up at PopUp Bagels in Lincoln Park, Saturday, May 30, 2026. PopUp’s debut was palpable. On St. Patrick’s Day, 400 people lined up for free PopUp bagels at a promotional popup at the Guinness Store House. The company declined to share details about its marketing budget or strategy, but Hadermann credited its “social media machine” for fostering a lot of excitement around openings. Influencers <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reel/DXVAP3_iUrD/" target="_blank" ><u>@eatwithseth</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reels/DXZQ8mGDvjB/" target="_blank" ><u>@artsialexi</u></a> were offered QR codes to skip the line and retrieve free bagels and limited-edition giardiniera cream cheese, made in collaboration with Portillo’s.</p><p>“I had no idea it was going to be bonkers, I just said OK I will try some bagels,” said local food writer and former pizza maker <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/dickholedannis/" target="_blank" ><u>Dennis Lee</u></a>, who was also invited. “There was a PR lady up front handling us; about two minutes later I had all these bagels.”</p><p>On a recent Friday morning, I waited about four minutes before placing my order, amid a steady stream of students, young parents and people in workout clothes.</p><p>PopUp’s bagels arrive hot and whole in packs of three, six or 12, plus schmear ($15, $24 or $48). My chubby little everything bagel sported a thin, crackly shell, nice seasoning and a pleasant stretchy-soft interior. Swiping pieces through tangy, vegetal spinach artichoke cream cheese reminded me of my grandpa, who used to slice off individual bagel pieces and slather them with salted butter.</p><p>Lee too called the eating experience “a joy,” but noted that the bagels, which are baked throughout the day and served hot, were already somewhat stale by the time he got home. (The company posts explicit reheating <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DA_j4laOO1C/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><u>instructions</u></a> on its social media).</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d50000" name="image-d50000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4296fc6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6141x3446+0+367/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff3%2Fd4%2F360009f0407786f6b1b6ccc6e0f2%2Fbagels-260603-4.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/da8d131/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6141x3446+0+367/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff3%2Fd4%2F360009f0407786f6b1b6ccc6e0f2%2Fbagels-260603-4.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f080cf2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6141x3446+0+367/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff3%2Fd4%2F360009f0407786f6b1b6ccc6e0f2%2Fbagels-260603-4.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A customer carries bags of PopUp Bagels in Lincoln Park, Saturday, May 30, 2026. Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Bagels striking enough for a photoshoot</b></h3><p>I thought about that comment a few days later, while driving to pick up a half dozen bagels and cream cheese ($25) from Rosca (Spanish for “ring”), the carryout-only spot inside bottled cocktail maker Hoste’s production facility and event space.</p><p>Chef and owner Felix Zepeda’s hand-rolled bagels start with hand-ground, locally sourced wheat berries and take three days to make. Featuring a thick crust with satisfying snap and interior chew, they’re liberally seasoned with the flavors that color Zepeda’s native Pilsen and Mexican heritage. Nutty, smoky-sweet red mole infuses the bagel of the same name, which is thickly shellacked with black and white sesame seeds. I vowed we’d return to try Zepeda’s hibiscus-cured lox as soon as we’d dispatched our half dozen.</p><p>I’m less sure when I’ll revisit PopUp, which will no doubt open much closer to my house someday soon.</p>

entries.title: Nearly 7-foot Obama sculpture welcomes visitors to presidential center
entries.summary: <p>The Obama Presidential Center officially opens in two weeks. And when it does, you'll be able to check out what'll likely be one of its most popular attractions without ever entering a building there.</p><p>A 1,200-lb bronze sculpture that memorializes former President Barack Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama's historic walk down crowd-lined Pennsylvania Avenue on Inauguration Day in 2009 stands on the center's entry plaza, right outside the front door of the Museum Tower.</p><p>The waving Obamas have already become a thirst trap for selfies and other photo-takers. During my visit to the center last week, people were touching the sculpture, shaking its hands and posing for pictures in front of it.</p><p>The piece was created by StudioEIS, a 50-year-old Brooklyn sculpture and design company. Their presidential work includes a striding John F. Kennedy at the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C., a Thomas Jefferson statue at the Virginia State Capitol in Richmond and a seated Franklin D. Roosevelt for the National WWII Museum in New Orleans.</p><p>"We just thought that President Obama was a young and vigorous president, and therefore, the photographs of the Obamas walking down Pennsylvania Avenue seemed a kind of fitting image that would endure for a very long time," StudioEIS founder and Director Ivan Schwartz said.</p><p>The firm pored over hundreds of Inauguration Day photos supplied by the Obama Foundation, looking for ones that were "a suitable interpretation" of the historic moment, Schwartz said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams dishes to Kelces about discovering tavern-style pizza
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/03/bears-caleb-williams-madden-27-cover-revealed-quarterback-video-game-nfl-ea-sports" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a> has a new Chicago food obsession: tavern-style pizza.</p><p>He told “New Heights” podcast hosts Jason and Travis Kelce about trying the square-cut pizza with the cracker-thin crust on Wednesday, shouting out Zarella downtown.</p><p>“Honestly,” he said, “the best pizza I’ve had in my life.”</p><p>The Kelces asked Williams whether he keeps up with the members of his draft class — the Commanders’ Jayden Daniels, the Patriots’ Drake Maye, the Falcons’ Michael Penix, the Vikings’ J.J. McCarthy and the Broncos’ Bo Nix.</p><p>“We gotta play vs. each other at some point …” he said. “There’s not too much communication going on.”</p><p>They follow each other on social media, Williams said, but check in just occasionally. The Bears play the Vikings, Falcons and Patriots this year, all in the first half of the season. Williams noted that the Bears have the hardest schedule in the NFL, in terms of last year’s opponent winning percentage.</p><p>“We’re excited,” he said. “We don’t back down from no challenge.”</p><p>Williams joked about Johnson taking off his shirt after beating the Eagles, saying he bulked up in the weight room beforehand, talked about how competitive swimming helped him as a kid.</p><p>The quarterback told the Kelces that returning to OTAs was easier this year than last because Ben Johnson’s offense was no longer brand new.</p><p>“It’s a lot better coming back and you know the plays and have an idea of the plays,” he said.<br></p>

entries.title: Boy, 1, safe after found in stolen vehicle on Far South Side
entries.summary: <p>A 1-year-old boy was found safe after a vehicle he was in was stolen early Wednesday on the Far South Side. </p><p>A 36-year-old man was next to his vehicle around 2:10 a.m. in the 9100 block of South Urban Avenue when someone got inside and drove away with the child, Chicago police said. </p><p>The boy was later found unharmed in the vehicle, in the 6200 block of South Eberhart Avenue, police said. </p><p>The boy was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center for observation, officials said. </p><p>Area detectives were investigating. </p>
