entries.title: YMCA offers free summer memberships to Chicago teens, 'safe spaces to meet'
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson has argued repeatedly that investing in young people — not throwing the book at them and their parents — is the answer to the perennial problem of teen takeovers. </p><p>On Wednesday, the mayor got a big assist in that effort, courtesy of the YMCA of Metropolitan Chicago.</p><p>Seven “Ys” across the city — Irving Park, Kelly Hall, Lake View, McCormick, Rauner Family, South Side and West Garfield Park — are offering free summer memberships to thousands of teens between the age of 12 and 18.</p><p>Starting Monday and continuing through Aug. 31, young people between the ages of 12 and 18 can walk into any one of those YMCAs and get a free membership card. They simply need proof of residency and need to be accompanied by an adult.</p><p>Adam Alonso, president and CEO of the YMCA of Metropolitan Chicago, said there’s too much talk about teen takeovers and not enough about “teen opportunity" and giving young people "safe spaces to meet and connect.”</p><p>“That should be our narrative. Not everything that’s wrong. Not everything that’s broken. But what’s right, what’s available to our young people,” Alonso told reporters at the South Side YMCA, 6330 S. Stony Island Ave.</p><p>“This is an opportunity to step into the moment and lead... Sign up, bring your friends... Use our fitness centers, our pools, our gyms, our fields, completely free of charge.”</p><p>Alonso acknowledged being “a little bit nervous because we’ve never done this.” He’s hoping as many as 5,000 young people take advantage of the free membership opportunity.</p><p>“I don’t know what’s going to happen," Alonso added. "We might have 10,000 young people show up and sign up. That would be an amazing problem to have.”</p><p>The number of takers could be on the high end if restless teens hear the sales pitch delivered by 18-year-old Maurice Allen. He’s been coming to the Y every day since he was a shy high school freshman.</p><p>“I started because I love sports — all sports. But what kept me coming back was everything else, Allen said. "The teen programs, the people. My friends are there... We play basketball. We work out. We hang out. It became my place.”</p><p>Allen said the teen program changed his life by helping a shy kid who wasn’t very social make “real friends, come out of my shell,” and prepare for adult responsibilities.</p><p>“The Y helped me get my Social Security job. It helped me prepare for a job interview at Wendy’s. And I got the job. They arranged my transportation to get there. Now they’re helping me learn how to drive. Whatever you need, they find a way to help make it happen,” Allen said.</p><p>Johnson joked that if he had known the Y offered free driving lessons, “I would have dropped my son off.”</p><p>Turning serious — and a bit emotional — the mayor recalled the days when he worked for the Y and saw how summer program fees “made it hard for some families” living in Cabrini Green.</p><p>“Young people would come into the Y and, unfortunately, were not able to stay and participate in programming because their parents did not have enough to feed them and provide opportunities for them,” the mayor said.</p><p>“And so, for all of those individuals that want to point fingers at our young people and point fingers at our families — if you do not know what it’s like to wake up in Chicago and you can barely make the ends meet, then stop judging our families and stop judging our young people. Stop it.”</p><p>After a Memorial Day weekend marred by teen takeovers turned violent, City Council support is building for a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/01/21/brian-hopkins-curfew-ordinance-new-revision-mayor-brandon-johnson-teen-takeovers" target="_blank" >revised curfew ordinance,</a> additional parental responsibility measures and for an attempt to hold social media companies accountable.</p><p>But Johnson reiterated Wednesday that the better answer is “life-changing” opportunities like summer jobs and the YMCA's offer of free summer membership.</p><p>“These partnerships… play a role in how we reduce violence,” he said.</p><p>As a preacher’s son and a self-declared “person of faith,” Johnson said he is “living out the creed of what Jesus Christ said.”</p><p>“We do not reject young people. We do not turn them away… We can hold young people accountable. They want to be held accountable. But if you do not provide opportunity for young people, then you are rejecting young people,” he said.</p>
entries.author: Fran Spielman

entries.title: Former Young, Loyola star Lucas Williamson received a taste of the NBA this season
entries.summary: <p>With the NBA G League season completed in late March, Lucas Williamson’s mind was locked in on coaching.</p><p>Following his fourth G League season, the local star, who led Whitney Young to a state championship in 2017 and was instrumental in helping Loyola to the Final Four in 2018, was set to coach his former high school travel team, Meanstreets, on Nike’s EYBL circuit.</p><p>Williamson flew home from his final G League game with the Windy City Bulls on Mar. 28. The next day he packed up his hotel room where he had been staying in Schaumburg, jumped in his car and was driving home to Chicago when his agent called.</p><p>“I answered the phone and he said to me, ‘I don’t want to get your hopes up, but there is a chance you will be getting called up to the [Memphis] Grizzlies,’” Williamson said his agent told him.</p><p>Williamson paused, asked his agent if he was serious, and then said if there was a legitimate chance, he would be heading straight to the gym to make sure he was ready if the call came. Off to the gym he went to get a workout in.</p><p>“At the time I was thinking about taking two weeks off of basketball, focusing completely on the coaching because we had a tournament the next weekend,” Williamson said of his Meanstreets schedule. “That was the mindset I was in — full coaching mode.”</p><p>But two days after that call from his agent he was back on a plane, headed to Memphis, set to make his NBA debut against the New York Knicks.</p><p>“It was surreal,” Williamson said of the NBA call-up. “I think it was surreal, not because of who I was looking at on the floor or who I was playing with or against. It was more so knowing my journey. The red carpet wasn’t rolled out for me. I knew it wouldn’t be. I was expecting my path to be hard. But I wasn’t expecting it to be this hard.”</p><p>In the previous three seasons, Williamson suffered season-ending injuries in two of them. The one that ended his 2024-25 season led him to question whether he was even going to continue playing basketball. But the 6-4 guard has never let hardships dictate his path.</p><p>Early on in his career it was easy to identify how Williamson would handle adversity. His former high school coach, Tyrone Slaughter, recognized quickly how his bright, young player was never self-absorbed. Slaughter says he never heard Williamson complain and that he was never afraid of the work, always doing so without any promises given to him.</p><p>“There was no job too small or too big for him,” said his former high school coach Tyrone Slaughter. “So when you talk about going through the G League and staying with it after injuries and not giving up — and I”m sure there were times where he may have wanted to give up — he leaned back into what he always has been. He leaned into his willingness to work hard.”</p><p>Following his highly-successful high school career, Loyola head coach Drew Valentine witnessed Williamson’s perseverance firsthand. He coached Williamson for five seasons — first as an assistant and then as the head coach after taking over for Porter Moser.</p><p>“Ever since I met Lucas he’s been a person who has just been incredibly process oriented,” Valentine said. “Most people, especially nowadays, want instant gratification, instant microwavable success. For him, everything has been step by step and process-driven. He’s never allowed adversity to get in the way of his process or the belief he has in himself.”</p><p>Williamson took a step back last summer and sat down with his agent to discuss his future. He came to the conclusion that he didn’t want to be 50 or 60 years old and wake up wondering if he pulled the plug too quickly on his career.</p><p>“I believed I still had the tools that impact winning,” Williams said. “I have an immense belief and confidence in myself of what I can bring to a team. I decided to go back to the G League.”</p><p>The grind of being a basketball vagabond in the NBA G League is a chore to navigate.</p><p>This past season, he admits, was not one of his better ones. His shooting numbers were down. He didn’t see eye-to-eye with his Memphis Hustle coach, which included a couple of self-described “run-ins,” before he was traded. His confidence had slipped.</p><p>“There is a lot that comes with it,” Williamson said of playing in the G League. “There is an immense mental load you’re dealing with in the G League. The G officially stands for Gatorade, but the G really stands for the grind. I was struggling.”</p><p>The trade to the Windy City Bulls from the Memphis Hustle was a blessing. He was soon playing more minutes, finally getting into a rhythm, and the confidence returned. With the confidence, along with all the winning attributes he brings to a team, there was a bit of a mini, late-season renaissance for Williamson.</p><p>“The hope is, the thing that keeps you going, is that you are one call away from your dream,” Williamson said of playing in the G League.</p><p>Williamson scored two points in eight minutes in that NBA debut against the Knicks. Overall, in the seven games with Memphis to close the season, he averaged a whopping 32 minutes a game while putting up 10.4 points a game.</p><p>Williamson said all he was concerned about was focusing on the opportunity that was given and to try and take advantage of it. He was of the belief that he simply needed to go out and perform and then let other people — coaches, scouts, front offices — do their job in seeing the value he brings.</p><p>But he also made sure to appreciate the experience, knowing how unparalleled of a basketball opportunity this was for him.</p><p>“I looked at it as this is special and I am taking in every single moment,” Williamson said of his two weeks in the NBA. “Being one of less than 5,000 players to have ever played in the NBA is super humbling.”</p><p>While he waits to see what happens next in his playing career, hoping his brief NBA run opened eyes, Williamson is back in the gym, simultaneously training for what might be ahead for him as a player while also coaching Meanstreets’ 16U team.</p><p>Williamson said he first heard of the opportunity to coach with Meanstreets in January. He was immediately intrigued by what program director Tim Anderson, who coached Williamson during his own Meanstreets days, had to say.</p><p>“It was honestly something I couldn’t pass up and just made a lot of sense,” Williamson said. “It was a program I was a part of, and I liked the idea of doing my best in giving back what I’ve learned.”</p><p>Valentine isn’t surprised to see Williamson honing his skills as a coach.</p><p>“I’ve always viewed Lucas as someone who would be a leader of men,” Valentine said.</p><p>Williamson says he enjoys coaching. He loves the preparation and the adrenaline he gets before games. The 27-year-old will keep the door — and his mind — open to the possibility of a coaching career.</p><p>“Right now I want to pay it forward, especially with this program,” Williamson said of coaching with Meanstreets. “I wouldn’t be at Loyola if it wasn’t for Meanstreets. And if I’m not at Loyola, then none of this happens.”<br></p>
entries.author: Joe Henricksen

entries.title: Late Cubs Hall of Famer Ryne Sandberg's family embroiled in lawsuit over handling of his trust
entries.summary: <p>The late Cubs legend Ryne Sandberg’s children are suing his widow over alleged violations of his trust.</p><p>Ryne Sandberg, a Hall of Famer who was known as "Ryno" and may be best remembered for his iconic performance on June 23, 1984 aka the “Sandberg Game,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2025/07/28/hall-of-famer-and-cubs-legend-ryne-sandberg-passes-away-after-battle-with-prostate-cancer" target="_blank" ><u>died last summer</u></a> at age 65 of metastatic prostate cancer.</p><p>In a civil lawsuit filed in Lake County district court, Ryne Sandberg’s son Justin and daughter Lindsey from his first marriage accused his second wife, Margaret Sandberg, of trying to shift control of his name, image and likeness to his stepson and the family financial advisor shortly before he passed away.</p><p>Before his death, Sandberg penned a document that would establish a publicity rights trust after his death to control his name, image and likeness. Justin Sandberg, Lindsey Sandberg Newton and Margaret Sandberg were named as trustees.</p><p>But Margaret Sandberg never responded to her stepchildren when they tried to set up the trust, and it was never created, in what Justin Sandberg and Lindsey Sandberg Newton are calling a “direct contravention” to their dad’s wishes, according to the complaint, first filed in April.</p><p>After divorcing his first wife Cindy, Sandberg married Margaret Koehnemann in August 1995.</p><p>The family’s financial advisors also tried twice to open a bank account where Ryne Sandberg’s publicity rights checks would be deposited. His children filled out the necessary documents, but Margaret Sandberg did not, and no bank account has been opened, the lawsuit says.</p><p>Further, Margaret Sandberg showed them a note earlier this year purportedly written by Ryne Sandberg before his death. The note identifies Margaret Sandberg’s son from a previous marriage, Steven Koehnemann (who was Ryne Sandberg's stepson), and the family financial advisor, Kathy Lintz, as part of the “NIL committee,” referring to the name, image and likeness of Ryne Sandberg.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a complaint, Ryne Sandberg’s children allege the note isn’t a valid amendment to his trust because it wasn’t presented to them until months after it was written and because any changes to the trust require the consent of the trustees. The trust can’t be altered to increase obligations or decrease compensation of the trustees without the consent of all of them, the complaint says.</p><p>They also point out that the note was dated four days before their dad entered hospice in July 2025 and that he was in severe physical pain and mental anguish, calling into question his ability to make decisions about his trust. During this time, Ryne Sandberg was heavily medicated and it was difficult to hold conversations with him, the complaint says. The note was dated the same day Lindsey Sandberg Newton heard her dad screaming out in pain, the complaint says.</p><p>Sandberg died July 28, 20025.</p><p>In the trust document, Ryne Sandberg implored his first two children and second wife to work together to make decisions.</p><p>“It would disappoint me if they were unable to make decisions on my NIL in a positive and collaborative manner,” Ryne Sandberg wrote in the trust document, according to the complaint. “It is also important to me to have any project reflect positively on my legacy and my entire family.”</p><p>Margaret Sandberg could not be reached for comment. Norm Finkel, an attorney for Justin Sandberg and Lindsey Sandberg Newton, didn’t respond to a request for comment.</p>

entries.title: White Sox giving away Caleb Williams bobbleheads in September
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/03/bears-qb-caleb-williams-travis-jason-kelce-new-heights-podcast-dishes-tavern-style-pizza" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a> is getting a bobblehead.</p><p>The White Sox will give away a Williams bobblehead before their game against the Twins on Sept. 6, the last Sunday before the start of the NFL season. The bobblehead shows the quarterback in White Sox black and silver uniform with a White Sox logo on the sleeve. It requires a game special ticket that must be purchased through the White Sox.</p><p>Williams began the Caleb Cares Foundation while playing quarterback at USC, teaming up with the Boys & Girls Club. He has since put on events near his hometown in the Washington, D.C., area as well as in Chicago. He was named the NFLPA’s Community MVP for Week 11 last year after hosting 40 youth football players for a weekend in Chicago.</p><p>This won’t be Williams’ first bobblehead. In 2023, following his Heisman Trophy-winning for the Trojans, Williams got the bobblehead treatment from the Los Angeles Dodgers.<br></p>

entries.title: Agentes de ICE paralizan a un hombre con taser y embisten su auto en un arresto caótico en Albany Park
entries.summary: <p>Agentes federales que perseguían y detenían a un hombre la mañana del martes en Albany Park chocaron contra el auto de una mujer durante la persecución y amenazaron a los residentes que se reunieron en la caótica escena.</p><p>Un reportero de Sun-Times fue testigo del suceso y de sus consecuencias.</p><p>El arresto ocurre en medio de un esfuerzo continuo por parte de las autoridades de inmigración federal para realizar arrestos en el área de Chicago, meses después del final del Operativo Midway Blitz, la campaña de deportación intensa de la administración de Trump que resultó en miles de arrestos.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-660000" name="module-660000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Desde el comienzo de este año hasta mediados de marzo, se han detenido a 580 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/05/08/equipos-de-respuesta-rapida-de-chicago-cambian-tacticas-ante-baja-visibilidad-de-control-migratorio" target="_blank" >personas en el área de Chicago</a><u>,</u> según un análisis de Sun-Times/WBEZ de datos del Proyecto de Datos de Deportación.</p><p>El incidente del martes comenzó a las 8:07 a.m., cuando un agente en una SUV Nissan negra giró hacia el este en Lawrence Avenue de Kedzie Avenue, persiguiendo a un hombre sin camisa. Una segunda Nissan SUV negra, con más agentes a bordo, salió de un estacionamiento cercano y chocó contra el auto de una mujer en un aparente intento de bloquear al hombre.</p><p>Los agentes llevaban insignias y parches del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) asociados con el Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE).</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/ysQNeEB3ecE?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="ICE agents shock man with Taser, barrel into car during chaotic arrest in Albany Park"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Tres agentes finalmente derribaron al hombre al suelo mientras este gritaba pidiendo ayuda y a los agentes que lo soltaran, mientras lo mantenían bajo la defensa delantera de una de las SUV. Luego, un agente le aplicó una descarga eléctrica con un taser.</p><p>El agente también apuntó el arma hacia los transeúntes y hacia un periodista. Otro agente sacó un aerosol de gas pimienta y lo apuntó a la multitud mientras alejaba a los vehículos que pasaban.</p><p>Durante la pelea, un agente dejó caer un cargador de balas completamente cargado en la calle. Un supervisor lo recogió minutos después, tras la salida de otros agentes.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a8cfff" name="image-a8cfff"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c05e5df/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1596x896+0+356/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc7%2F64%2Ff530a5e140f7bf74dd67c062a9f0%2Falbanyparkice-260603-2-2c.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fcd629a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1596x896+0+356/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc7%2F64%2Ff530a5e140f7bf74dd67c062a9f0%2Falbanyparkice-260603-2-2c.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0d3cdcf/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1596x896+0+356/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc7%2F64%2Ff530a5e140f7bf74dd67c062a9f0%2Falbanyparkice-260603-2-2c.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Un cargador con munición en vivo se encuentra en la acera al oeste de Lawrence Avenue, tras dejarla caer un agente federal mientras detenía a un hombre el martes. Un supervisor regresó a la escena unos minutos después para recuperarla.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Violet Miller/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Mientras detenían al hombre, los agentes amenazaron con arrestar a la mujer cuyo auto había sido golpeado. Había estado detenida en un semáforo en rojo.</p><p>Unas docenas de personas se presentaron y se enfrentaron a los siete agentes federales que llegaron en cinco vehículos sin identificar equipados con luces de emergencia. Los testigos grabaron con sus teléfonos celulares, usaron silbatos y les gritaron a los agentes.</p><p>Un agente tenía una calcomanía de la cruz de Jerusalén en la parte posterior de su teléfono, un símbolo cristiano que data de las Cruzadas y que más recientemente ha ganado popularidad entre <a class="Link" href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-51118025" target="_blank" >grupos de extrema derecha y supremacistas blancos</a>. El Secretario de Defensa Pete Hegseth <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-defense-department-pentagon-hegseth-fox-news-8cd9f065e54a7cbbaceeec8bae9261a6" target="_blank" >fue criticado</a> por tener un tatuaje en el pecho de una cruz de Jerusalén en las semanas previas a la segunda inauguración del presidente Donald Trump.</p><p>Los oficiales de la Policía de Chicago que llegaron minutos después del arresto hablaron con testigos y redactaron un reporte de policía. Un oficial dijo que los detectives se encargarían de la investigación si el choque se consideraba un atropello y fuga.</p><p>“[Los agentes] no querían mostrarnos prueba de eso”, le dijo un oficial a la mujer cuyo auto fue golpeado.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d77cef" Los agentes estaban persiguiendo a un hombre al que pronto arrestaron y luego le dieron una descarga eléctrica con una pistola taser.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Violet Miller/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>DHS y ICE no respondieron a una solicitud de comentarios.</p><p>Cuando los agentes federales abandonaron la escena, condujeron hacia el sur hacia el vecindario de Irving Park.</p><p>En un <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/33rdward/videos/1977625382872710/" target="_blank" >video publicado en redes sociales</a><u>,</u> la concejal Rossana Rodríguez Sánchez (33.º) confirmó que el hombre fue detenido y advirtió a los residentes mientras las escuelas cercanas realizaban actividades al aire libre. Rodríguez Sánchez sospechaba que los vehículos federales habían estado estacionados y circulando cerca de la Escuela Primaria Haugan la mañana anterior.</p><p>“Se llevaron a un vecino de Kedzie y Lawrence”, dijo. “Estamos tratando de estar atentos a todo porque hoy hay algunas graduaciones y días de campo. Por favor, tengan cuidado, cuídense si son vulnerables, están afuera en la comunidad en este momento".</p><p>El vecindario de Albany Park ha sido escenario de arrestos migratorios previos.</p><p>El incidente del martes ocurrió en la misma intersección donde los agentes federales <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/10/28/residentes-del-noroeste-enfrentan-a-agentes-que-disparan-gas-lacrimogeno-cancelan-desfile-de-halloween" target="_blank" >detuvieron a un hombre en Halloween</a> en octubre mientras disparaban bolas de gas pimienta a los residentes. lacrimógeno</a> dos semanas antes.</p><p>Los residentes vieron a agentes de ICE vigilar áreas desde sus vehículos el día anterior, tratando de detener a alguien, dijo Erika Husby, residente de Albany entries.title: Chicago’s cultural department launches new grant progam aimed at helping emerging theater companies
entries.summary: <p>Chicago’s cultural department announced a new grant program Wednesday aimed at helping emerging theater organizations strengthen their infrastructure and build audiences.</p><p>The program, Next Stage Chicago, will provide a maximum of $50,000 to up to eight nonprofit theater companies that have been in business for at least three years but no more than 10. Cultural commissioner Kenya Merritt said the $400,000 program is an investment in organizations that are “essential to the vitality of Chicago’s neighborhoods.”</p><p>“If we want Chicago to remain one of the great cultural cities, we must invest in it,” Merritt said during a City Club Chicago event on Wednesday. “Next Stage is just one example of that commitment, and it is only the beginning.”</p><p>Merritt, a former deputy mayor in the Johnson administration, was confirmed to lead the Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events in mid-April and has repeatedly stressed that she believes the arts sector can be an economic driver for the city.</p><p>“The arts are economic infrastructure. The arts are a workforce strategy. The arts are a neighborhood strategy,” Merritt said Wednesday.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Events in mid-April.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Grantmaking has long been a core tenet of the department, in addition to its role in organizing large-scale downtown events such as this weekend’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2026/06/02/chicago-blues-festival-alligator-records-bruce-iglauer-lil-ed-williams-55-anniversary" target="_blank" ><u>Blues Festival</u></a>.</p><p>Next Stage Chicago will give funds to organizations “that are actively building their audiences, strengthening their infrastructure and expanding their artistic impact,” according to the city.</p><p>Chicago’s robust storefront theater scene has <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/culture-the-arts/2024/04/22/chicago-actors-wages-non-equity-storefront" target="_blank" ><u>gained global acclaim</u></a>, but in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, many arts organizations — especially smaller companies — have struggled to draw audiences back to live performances.</p><p>The DCASE grant dollars (funding for which came, in part, from a Pritzker Foundation grant) can be used for “organizational management, marketing and audience development, financial planning and development, production management, and strategic planning.”</p><p>Eligible applicants must have an annual operating budget of $500,000 or less and “demonstrate a commitment to producing and presenting theatrical work.”</p><p>Across multiple programs, DCASE gives grants to both arts organizations and individual artists annually. In 2025, the department awarded a little more than $10 million in grants to about 650 recipients, according to public records. That was up from the slightly more than <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2024/11/13/chicago-arts-funding-city-budget-dcase-culture-artist-grants" target="_blank" ><u>$8 million</u></a> in grants the year before. The department’s grantmaking swelled during the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2025/01/13/chicago-arts-funding-trump-grants-dcase-individual-artists-program-iap" target="_blank" ><u>more than $22 million in 2023</u></a>.</p><p></p><p>In recent years, arts funding has been under attack federally. Last year, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2025/05/06/nea-grants-trump-chicago-cultural-events" target="_blank" ><u>National Endowment for the Arts</u></a> canceled grant dollars that had already been awarded, including to arts organizations locally. In the aftermath, the city stepped in to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2025/07/29/chicago-arts-grants-dcase-nea-federal-cultural-funding-trump" target="_blank" ><u>provide grants</u></a> to arts groups that had lost federal funding.</p><p>During the latest budget battle at City Hall, DCASE’s budget was <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/city-hall/2025/11/05/chicago-dcase-cultural-affairs-budget-clinee-hedspeth-kenya-merritt-grants-arts" target="_blank" ><u>decreased by 15%</u></a>.</p><p>Applications for Next Stage Chicago are now open and close at noon on Wednesday, July 8. Recipients will be notified in September, and payments will be issued in December, according to the city.</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ.</i></p>

entries.title: Review: “Andy Warhol Presents: The Cocaine Play”
entries.summary: <p>When I think of Andy Warhol, two things come to mind: Campbell’s soup and Marilyn Monroe. Even though the prolific artist and filmmaker died in the late 1980s, he remains legendary, with many of us still having at least a passing knowledge of his contributions to pop culture.</p><p>I have no idea how close actor William Anthony Sebastian Rose II (Jeff Award winner for “Tambo & Bones”) came to embodying the actual Warhol in his titular role in Terry Guest’s “Andy Warhol Presents: The Cocaine Play,” but it doesn’t matter. His performance was captivating.</p><p>This world premiere, written and directed by Guest, and running at Jackalope Theatre through July 6, introduces the audience to a fictionalized Warhol, Marilyn Monroe (Alexis Ward), and Edie Sedgwick (Jasmine “Jazzy” Cheri Rush). As the title suggests, there is plenty of cocaine, alongside the story of struggling artists grappling with the cost of success.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="3.5" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> “Andy Warhol Presents: The Cocaine Play” </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e50000" name="module-e50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When</b>: Through July 6<br><b>Where</b>: Jackalope Theatre at Broadway Armory Park, 5917 N. Broadway St.<br><b>Info</b>: <a class="Link" href="https://www.jackalopetheatre.org/andy-warhol-presents-the-cocaine-play" target="_blank" ><u>Tickets from $15</u></a></div> </div><p>We meet a young, up-and-coming version of Warhol in 1960s New York City. But he has a problem: He hasn’t been able to complete a painting in a very long time. His best friend, and lover, the painter Michael Brown (David Michael Dowd), offers him an opportunity. He lands a gallery show and gives Warhol a slot. By chance, Warhol meets young actress Marilyn Monroe, who inspires him to create a painting — “Marilyn Diptych” — which launches Warhol into superstardom and leaves Brown in the dust.</p><p>The ensuing drama is an epic tale of love, passion and betrayal that examines the cost of fame and fortune. How far will an artist go to become a legend? And, once success is achieved, is it even worth it?</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Photography</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The characters here all have problems associated with varying levels of success. Brown helped Warhol when he was down and out, yet when the opportunity arose for the favor to be returned he’s shunned. This leads to a deep seeded jealousy that manifests over years, with Brown feeling like he is owed something he couldn’t have, and as we later learn, perhaps didn’t deserve.</p><p>Both Monroe and Sedgwick go through the ringer as actresses. Monroe, who is already successful when introduced, is typecast and only viewed through the lens of her beauty, not her true artistry. Her fate is to be immortalized, but not in the way she wishes. Meanwhile, Sedgwick is never taken seriously and after commercials become the easiest gigs to get, she’s reduced to being known as the girl who sings the Mr. Coffee jingle.</p><p>All of the characters, even the rich and famous Warhol, are doomed. And while the journey of the production is enjoyable, with legit laugh out loud moments, it is a tragedy. Guest explores the pitfalls of being an artist and offers a glimpse into their sometimes troubled inner lives.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>All of the characters, even the rich and famous Warhol, are doomed.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Joel Maisonet/Maisonet Photography</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The production spans three decades and boasts a run time of well over two hours with two intermissions. I’m usually not a fan of shows this long, but here it works. Dowd is excellent as Brown, delivering an agonizing performance as he slips into despair over decades of not achieving the success that was once at his finger tips. Rush, fresh off an impressive performance in Guest’s “Oak,” is equally strong here as Sedgwick.</p><p>Rose is a force as the neurotic, flamboyant, coke-fueled Warhol. He breathes so much life into this character with a mixture of deft comedic timing and the ability to make an audience sit with heavy emotion. He’s scathing when necessary but also tender. And his wigs (designed by associate director Ayanna Bria Bakari) are a delight.</p><p>The impressive artistry of this production also goes beyond strong writing and acting. The lighting by Levi J. Wilkins and set design by Sydney Lynne Thomas pull this show together. The stage is framed like a portrait, and when the artists paint, they turn to face the audience. Lights flash in corresponding colors, bringing the audience into the creative process, and giving us a sense that we’re inside a painting. It’s a good touch.</p><p>In real life, Warhol is credited with popularizing the idea that everyone will be famous for 15 minutes. But here’s the real question at the center of this play: Are those minutes worth your life?</p>

entries.title: Fired nurses allege retaliation for voicing concerns about conditions at St. Mary of Nazareth Hospital
entries.summary: <p>When Saint Mary of Nazareth Hospital was acquired by Prime Healthcare in March 2025, nurse Karlie Thorn said she noticed conditions in the emergency department changed for the worse almost immediately.</p><p>A disproportionate number of inexperienced nurses, cheaper supplies and staffing shortages were among the concerning conditions Thorn and several other nurses allege, alarming them enough to prompt considering unionization.</p><p>As staffers launched an effort to hold an election to unionize with National Nurses Organizing Committee/National Nurses United last month, at least six nurses were fired in what the union calls a "troubling pattern of going after experienced nurses who are advocating for their patients and coworkers." </p><p>“I think it sent a message to the nurses in our community that we’re expendable and when we speak up for each other, they’ll get rid of us with no just cause," said Thorn, one of the fired nurses. “We want an election that's fair and without interference from Prime, and we want our nurses back.”</p><p>“As nurses, we take care of everyone all day,” added Thorn, an emergency department nurse for the last four years. “We deserve to be taken care of as well.”</p><p>Registered nurses at Saint Mary's plan to hold a one-day strike on June 11 to protest what they is retaliation for speaking out about unsafe conditions, calling it a strike for “patient safety and an end to union busting.” The fired nurses are also petitioning to get their jobs back.</p><p>In a statement to the Sun-Times, a Saint Mary's spokesperson said, "we have not and will not retaliate against employees for exercising their rights and have consistently applied longstanding hospital policies that protect safety and patient care.”</p><p>“Saint Mary's of Nazareth Hospital respects the right of nurses to make their own decisions regarding union representation and to engage in lawful protected activity,” the statement said. Saint Mary's added that “comprehensive plans" were in place to ensure operations uninterrupted during the one-day strike.</p><p>Since Prime acquired Saint Mary's, along with seven other area hospitals, nurses at the Ukrainian Village hospital say they have felt overworked, fearful for their jobs and greater concerned for their safety and for that of their patients.</p><p>“We have always had staffing issues in the ER, but they have gotten worse since Prime took over,” Thorn said. “It’s just not safe for us to have 25 people in the waiting room and each nurse already has four to five patients.”</p><p>Patient ratios for emergency room nurses are typically one-to-five, Thorn noted, though more recently it has been seven patients for every nurse because of staff members who left because of concerns about hospital conditions or were fired.</p><p>Jesus Hernandez, a behavioral health nurse for the seven years before he was fired, said his unit has lost monitors, making it more difficult to care for patients quickly and leaving patients at risk of harming each other or staff members who are responding to a crisis.</p><p>“[The monitors] are kind of our eyes and ears on the behavioral health floor to make sure the patients and staff are safe,” Hernandez said. </p><p>Some older patients are at more likely to fall, while others without a safety attendant have impulses that could lead to physical aggression, he said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-db0000" </div> </div><p>Amiee Bae worked for more than seven years in Saint Mary's acute male psychiatric unit before she she says she was fired for speaking out about poor conditions in her unit. Bae said the changes after Prime took over were small at first. </p><p>Things like lower-quailty gloves, patient socks and towels gave way to bigger changes, Bae said, including the loss of addiction medication that in some instances was life-saving for patients in the hospital's six psychiatric units.</p><p>“Alcohol withdrawal can kill somebody if you’re not treating them properly,” Bae said. “They can go into severe pain and distress.”</p><p>Though Bae has been a vocal critic of the changes she's seen since Prime took over, she said she’s still willing to work with the California-based healthcare company because of her passion for nursing. She hopes the strike leads to the fired nurses getting reinstated.</p><p>“I gave 200% of my soul, my physical capacity to St. Mary’s for seven years,” Bae said. </p><p>“I’m still willing to work with Prime because I love my hospital. I love who I serve.”</p>

entries.title: State Comptroller Mendoza enters mayoral race, takes shots at Mayor Johnson, Giannoulias
entries.summary: <p>Arguing that Chicago needs “competent leadership” — not a mayor who “coddles criminals” and is beholden to the Chicago Teachers Union —Illinois Comptroller Susana Mendoza on Wednesday officially joined the crowded race for mayor of Chicago.</p><p>Mendoza finished fifth in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/4/3/18349334/lightfoot-meets-with-emanuel-to-begin-transition-after-landslide-win" >2019 mayoral race</a> won by Lori Lightfoot that was dominated by the corruption scandal that culminated in the conviction of former Ald. Edward Burke (14th).</p><p>She won just seven of the 50 wards in 2019, nearly all of them majority Hispanic, and captured just over 9% of the vote. She was damaged heavily by her longstanding alliance with Burke and now-convicted Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan (D-Chicago).</p><p>But Mendoza told the Sun-Times she is a far more seasoned candidate than the one who finished behind Lightfoot, Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle, former White House Chief of Staff Bill Daley and perennial candidate Willie Wilson.</p> <p>Mendoza argued that her “trifecta of experience” as a state legislator, city clerk and state comptroller proves she is the “turnaround expert” Chicago needs to solve its financial and public safety troubles, along with its “crisis of confidence” under incumbent Brandon Johnson.</p><p>“We need a mayor who will not coddle criminals, but will hold them accountable and flip the moral compass on this city to put victims ahead of offenders. That’s a key point of failure for this administration,” said Mendoza, 54.</p><p>“The most obvious one that everybody feels… is the financial crisis that we’re in. And there is no one better situated to fix the city’s finances than somebody who fixed the state’s [finances] when many people thought it was an impossible task to do. That is my sweet spot.”</p><p>Mendoza’s $1.6 million campaign war chest pales by comparison to the<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/04/16/brandon-johnson-alexi-giannoulias-susana-mendoza-potential-mayoral-bids-campaign-fundraising" > $18.3 million </a>already amassed by Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias, a potential candidate for mayor.</p><p>But Mendoza, who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2025/07/16/susana-mendoza-chicago-mayor-comptroller-brandon-johnson" >opted not to run again</a> for comptroller this year, said she is not intimidated by Giannoulias’ prolific fundraising or big contributions he has received from building trade unions. She added she will not be muscled out of the race by a candidate who appears to be playing it safe by remaining on the sidelines.</p><p>“Isn't he running for secretary of state? He hasn’t declared [for mayor]. I’m running for mayor of Chicago and I don’t care who gets in this race,” she said.</p><p>“No one can touch me on my financial experience. No one can touch me on my know-how in getting things done in Springfield… I don’t have to ask anyone for permission to put my thoughts out there. I’m going to run this city better than any other executive manager has in the past. And you can take that to the bank. Just not Broadway Bank,” the now-shuttered bank once owned by the Giannoulias family, and that once employed him. </p><p>Johnson has not yet declared his intention to seek a second term. His approval rating is languishing in the low 30s, and he has just $813,125 in campaign cash on hand. </p><p>His ability to raise money is likely to be hampered by the recent decision by the rank-and-file of the Chicago Teachers Union to reject the $8.5 million dues increase championed by CTU President Stacy Davis Gates.</p><p>But the embattled mayor still has the far left lane to himself, and is the only prominent African American candidate considering a run. </p><p>Mendoza and Giannoulias are vying for voters in the same moderate lane. That explains why Mendoza appeared to be taking as many shots at Giannoulias as she did at Johnson.</p><p>“I wasn’t born with a silver spoon in my mouth. I was born more [with] like a plastic spork and people relate to that. They know who’s legit. They know who can relate to them, who’s authentic,” she said. “There’s a big difference between that and somebody holding the doorman’s hand as he’s hitting the button to get him up their skyscraper.”</p><p>Giannoulias could not be reached for comment.</p><p>Johnson tried once again to remain above the political fray.</p><p>“No mayor in the modern history can say that they oversaw the city of Chicago at the height of economic development and activity, where more people are visiting our city than any other time in the history of Chicago. And we just experienced a 60-year low in homicides,” the mayor said. <br>“That’s the work that I’m doing and I’m going to continue to concentrate on that." </p><p>Veteran political operative Victor Reyes said Mendoza's fiery entry into the race could turn up the heat on Giannoulias to get off the sidelines and into the race. </p><p>"They're going to have to protect that flank. It can't be just all anti-Johnson. Eventually, they're going to have to beat Susana's numbers down," Reyes said. "Every day that they delay is an advantage for Johnson."</p>

entries.title: Miguel Vargas is delivering on his promise for White Sox
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS — Miguel Vargas is on pace for a career year, and his breakout couldn’t have come at a better time for the White Sox, who must navigate at least a month without slugger Munetaka Murakami.</p><p>Since Murakami and his team-high 20 home runs went on the injured list last Saturday, Vargas has hit in Murakami’s usual No. 2 spot in four of five games. Though Vargas’ place in the lineup can change depending on the pitching matchup, it’s clear that the Sox will lean on him regardless of who’s on the mound.</p><p>After the Sox’ 8-0 victory against the Twins on Wednesday, Vargas led all major-league third basemen with 15 homers, 41 RBI, 46 runs and 40 walks. He also ranked second in on-base percentage (.368) and tied for second in slugging percentage (.502).</p><p>“It’s impressive; you see it every night,” manager Will Venable said. “He’s extremely consistent in how he approaches his preparation. It’s showing up on the field. Obviously, he feels really good and confident up there, and he continues to give himself a chance.”</p><p>Vargas already is just one homer and 19 RBI shy of his career highs, which he set last season, his first full season with the Sox. General manager Chris Getz acquired him from the Dodgers in a three-team trade in July 2024. The Dodgers deemed Vargas, a former top prospect, expendable because Max Muncy was holding down third.</p><p>He still is — Muncy was third in the majors in OPS among third basemen (.855), one spot behind Vargas — but Vargas is proving to be a steal for the Sox, who sent Erick Fedde and Tommy Pham to the Cardinals and Michael Kopech to the Dodgers in the trade. They even got Fedde back this season, for what it’s worth.</p><p>“I’m being really consistent with [swing] decisions,” Vargas said. “That was the plan we had coming into this year, to trust my eyes more and swing a little bit more. I feel in a really good spot right now and hopefully keep feeling that way.”</p><p>First-year Sox hitting coach Derek Shomon knew Vargas had been a top prospect with the Dodgers and loosely followed his career as Shomon coached with the Twins and Marlins. In the offseason, he and assistant hitting coach Joel McKeithan visited Vargas in Miami for a couple of days to get acquainted and work together.</p><p>“He’s great. High energy,” Shomon said. “He’s a jokester. He likes to talk crap, but he wears it well. He’s a super-talented player, love watching him work through his checkpoints every day. When he feels like it’s going awry, he can get back in line quickly.</p><p>“He’s a true three-skilled player: contact ability, good swing decisions and he can do damage. What you’re seeing right now, I know the bat speed is up, but it’s really a continuation of the work that he did from the second half last year into the offseason and getting the lower half to be more efficient.”</p><p>Though Vargas’ homers and RBI were down in the second half last season, his on-base and slugging percentages shot up more than 50 points each. And this season, his OPB is up almost 50 points from last season, and his SLG is up more than 100 points.</p><p>Can Vargas carry the load that Murakami had been carrying in the 2 hole?</p><p>“He absolutely can,” Shomon said. “You can count on a good at-bat. He’s a total hitter. He’s gonna draw walks, he’s gonna limit [strikeouts], he’s done it with good swing decisions. He can move the ball forward line to line or in the sky, and he can leave the yard.”</p><p>He’s also another feather in the cap for Getz.</p><p>“We were confident that he was going to take another step forward from last year; he’s done that,” Getz said. “Obviously, there were all these ingredients that we felt were in there when we acquired him. And then you put on top of that just the acumen and the work ethic, it’s really aligned for him, and he’s been a great player for us this year.”<br></p>

entries.title: Bears CB Tyrique Stevenson leaning on offensive coaches for help
entries.summary: <p>Cornerback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/02/26/with-uncertainty-lingering-on-tyrique-stevenson-bears-must-consider-cornerback-options-in-nfl-draft" target="_blank" >Tyrique Stevenson</a> has spent part of his offseason talking to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> offensive coaches and hitting them with a hypothetical question — how would they attack him?</p><p>He’d never done it before. But he likes how it’s helped to hone his practice habits.</p><p>“I just want to know where I can get better to help this team,” he said after practice Wednesday, “and go out there and perform at a high level.”</p><p>Stevenson figures to start opposite Jaylon Johnson this year after the Bears let Nahshon Wright leave in free agency. The Bears didn’t have much need for Stevenson toward the end of last season — he didn’t participate in a single snap in the regular season finale.</p><p>He said the benching didn’t motivate him this offseason, and referenced his most famous gaffe — jawing at the Commanders crowd and misplaying a game-ending Hail Mary in 2024 — in his explanation why.</p><p>“I'm always motivated going into my offseason,” he said. “I’ll be real, that the Hail Mary was the top of the top, so I'm always motivated now. But, no, I just understand the coaches’ decision.”</p><p>Defensive backs coach Al Harris has been impressed.</p><p>“The young man that reported last year is so totally different than the young man that's reporting this year,” he said. “He's focused in, he's locked in.</p><p>“The small details. You can just tell by the questions that he's asking, the small details he's honing in on, whether it's his movements, whether it's, ‘Hey Coach, just get me to the ball,’ he's asking the right questions, and he's staying focused in.”</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Congressman tells Endeavor Health stop acting against unionizing nurses at Chicago-area hospitals
entries.summary: <p>Democratic U.S. Rep. Jesus “Chuy” Garcia is calling for Endeavor Health to reinstate two Evanston Hospital nurses who were fired allegedly for trying to unionize.</p><p><u>It’s illegal</u> for most private employers, including hospitals, to penalize workers for forming a union, according to the National Labor Relations Board, an independent federal agency that protects the right to organize.</p><p>Nurses at Evanston, Skokie, Glenbrook and Highland Park hospitals, which are part of Endeavor Health, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/05/08/endeavor-health-nurses-look-to-unionize-over-pay-cuts-staffing-conditions" target="_blank" ><u>started openly unionizing</u></a> this spring.</p><p>In a June 2 letter obtained by WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times, Garcia urged Endeavor CEO Gerald Gallagher to refrain from intimidating or retaliating against nearly 3,000 nurses who are <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/05/08/endeavor-health-nurses-look-to-unionize-over-pay-cuts-staffing-conditions" target="_blank" ><u>working to unionize</u></a> with the Teamsters Local 743 over pay cuts and what they say are unsafe working conditions.</p><p>“All workers should have the free and fair choice to join a union,” wrote Garcia, who has progressive organizing roots. “Endeavor must stop its unfair labor practices, reinstate the two terminated nurses from Evanston Hospital, and respect workers’ right to form a union, free of intimidation, retaliation, and other forms of illegal interference.”</p><p>Endeavor is one of the biggest hospital systems in the Chicago area, treating more than 1 million patients a year and employing more than 27,000 people, according to the health system.</p><p>The not-for-profit hospital operator had about $6.4 billion in revenue in 2025. </p><p>Nurses have cited pay cuts of $5 to $22 an hour and “severe understaffing as contributing to a stressful work environment,” Garcia wrote, citing WBEZ/Sun-Times reporting. The pay cuts have come as some executives receive bonuses, records show.</p><p>Gallagher <a class="Link" href="https://app.candid.org/profile/14586470/endeavor-health-87-4520691?activeTab=7" target="_blank" ><u>made just over $5 million</u></a> in 2024, including a $1.4 million bonus, as well as retirement and other “deferred” compensation, Endeavor’s most recent tax return shows. That year, the health system had a $494 million operating loss, much of it from <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2025/02/19/endeavor-health-fabio-ortega-settlements/" target="_blank" ><u>legal settlements</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://emma.msrb.org/P11844429-P11412902-P11855647.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>an audited financial statement</u></a> shows.</p><p><u>Three charges</u> have been filed with the National Labor Relations Board against Endeavor since March, Garcia said in the letter. They include accusations of retaliation or disciplinary action against workers “engaged in protected concerted activities” and putting them under surveillance.</p><p>An Endeavor spokesperson said the health system carefully reviews “each individual employment action to ensure compliance with all applicable laws. We fully respect the federally protected rights of our nurses to engage and make an informed choice about union representation. While respecting these rights, we must prioritize the safety, privacy and care of our patients and team members and maintain consistent enforcement of our workplace policies.”</p><p>The unionizing effort has included Endeavor’s legacy hospitals in the suburbs — Evanston, Skokie, Glenbrook and Highland Park hospitals, according to Tricia Poreda, one of the Endeavor nurses leading organizing efforts. Those hospitals were part of the system when it was known as NorthShore University HealthSystem, before it grew bigger through mergers. The goal is to organize nurses across Endeavor, Poreda said.</p><p>The two nurses who were fired in May were experienced senior nurses in the intensive-care unit at Evanston Hospital, according to Poreda, who said they were dropping off gift bags with union information to nurses in the hospital and identified themselves to security employees inside. After working their roughly 12-hour night shifts, they were suspended without pay, then fired for allegedly misrepresenting themselves for wearing their work badges and scrubs while also wearing a union T-shirt, Poreda said.</p><p>The firings have galvanized nurses, according to Poreda. She said many used to be afraid to even talk about forming a union but now have started a petition that about 1,000 people have signed to get their fired colleagues back to work.</p><p>“This was a movement to reincite that fear and control, and it's really had the opposite effect,” she said. “It’s just made nurses even more upset and more driven.”</p><p><i>Kristen Schorsch covers the health of the region for WBEZ.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/05/08/endeavor-health-nurses-look-to-unionize-over-pay-cuts-staffing-conditions" >Thousands of Endeavor Health nurses look to unionize over pay cuts, staffing conditions</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Could Packers star Micah Parsons return just in time for Bears game?
entries.summary: <p>Packers star Micah Parsons’ return from injury could be at home against the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" >Bears</a>.</p><p>The edge rusher told Green Bay reporters Wednesday that his torn left ACL, for which he had surgery five months ago, still needed another four months of healing.</p><p>If Parsons is cleared to practice, then, it would be in September. Players coming off such long layoffs typically practice for a couple weeks before hitting the field.</p><p>His return, then, could line up with the Bears’ Oct. 11 game at Lambeau Field. That would add yet another level of drama to a rivalry game that already has two coaches who don’t get along. The Bears ended the Packers’ season in the playoffs, too.</p><p>Parsons told reporters that he was more worried about the end of the season than the beginning of it. He said the “goal for me is to complete the season … and playoffs and pushing towards a championship.”</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Kids open time capsules sealed during the pandemic, design new ones to be opened in 5 years
entries.summary: <p>Children at the James R. Jordan Boys & Girls Club on the Near West Side gathered this week to open time capsules created by students living through the COVID-19 pandemic — and then they created their own memory boxes, set to be opened in 2031.</p><p>In 2021, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/10/27/22749825/youth-decorated-pandemic-time-capsules-sealed-in-downtown-ceremony" target="_blank" >The Boys & Girls Clubs of Chicago partnered with Living Record</a>, previously known as Once Upon Our Time Capsule, to work with students to document what they experienced through the time of lockdowns, quarantines and hybrid learning and collect them in time capsules the kids embellished themselves. </p><p>This year, a new crop of students opened those capsules, and were encouraged to reflect on what previous Club kids went through during the pandemic.</p><p>Angel Rivera, vice president of youth development at the Club, said the event Tuesday in the Club's gymnasium was meant to be a moment of “social emotional learning.”</p><p>“To kind of reflect on this past year — what was important to this year? — and trying to memorialize some of those things, we always feel is a worthwhile practice to have with our kids,” Rivera said.</p><p>While the children taking part Tuesday ranged from kindergarteners to high schoolers, most were too young to remember living through the height of the pandemic and had few personal experiences to attach to the uncovered boxes filled with gloves and masks.</p><p>But Mekhi, 17, a high school senior who was in sixth grade when lockdown began, recalls creating his own capsule.</p><p>“I do remember, like, one day throughout the summer they were like making me write down, 'Who's your favorite artist? What's your favorite color? How are you feeling today?' entries.title: Bears CB Kyler Gordon's injuries keeping him from offseason 'springboard'
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> slot cornerback Kyler Gordon wasn’t happy with his injury-riddled season last year, and neither was his coach. Gordon played only three games, went to injured reserve twice and battled groin, hamstring and calf problems.</p><p>Offseason workouts don’t seem to be going much better. Gordon remained out Wednesday with a soft-tissue injury. Speaking before practice, coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/05/29/bears-coach-ben-johnson-luther-burden-buying-stock-wide-receiver-dj-moore-organized-team-activity-missouri-second-year-nfl" target="_blank" >Ben Johnson</a> seemed frustrated.</p><p>“This spring was going to be a springboard for us to get going in the right direction,” Johnson said. “So, you know, we're still working through that. We're still trying to get that availability piece going.”</p><p>The Bears gave Gordon a three-year, $40 million extension in April 2025. The new coaching staff was excited about him — he was the only player defensive coordinator Dennis Allen mentioned by name in his opening press conference.</p><p>It’s clear, though, that they need to see him play more.</p><p>“We know he's a good player when he's out there,” Johnson said. “But trust level is a huge thing for this team, for this coaching staff, for the locker room and you can only develop that trust by being available.”</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>• Two veterans practiced during the individual portion Wednesday, a sign of progress — defensive end Dayo Odeyingbo (Achilles’ tendon) and linebacker T.J. Edwards (leg). Rookie cornerback Malik Muhammad joined them.</p><p>• The team that knocked the Bears out of the playoffs got even stronger earlier this week when the Rams traded for Browns superstar edge rusher Myles Garrett. Johnson, though, wasn’t interested in breaking down what it meant for the Bears and the rest of the NFC.<br>“Not a whole lot of thought goes into it,” he said. “We got our own business we’re taking care of right now.”</p><p>• The NFL announced the days and times of the Bears’ three preseason games: at noon Aug. 15 against the Browns, at 6 p.m. Aug. 22 in Cincinnati and at 5 p.m. Aug. 29 in Nashville. The league had previously announced the Browns, Bengals and Titans as opponents. Th Bears will practice against the Bengals on Aug. 20. Johnson said they were working to book another joint practice, too.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-bc0001" name="list-bc0001"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, pageNumber=1, inverseColors=false, footerBgColor=#000000, bodyFont=font-3, showListNumbers=false, imagePositionHorizontal=null, pageCount=6898, rteBodyFont=font-3, headerBottomBorderColor=#111010, titleUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears, subTitle=null, stickyHeader=true, listTitleColor=#000000, tableCellBorderColor=#ccd1d5, relatedListFont=font-1, hideAuthors=true, tertiaryTextColor=#6c6c6c, buttonHoverTextColor=#ffffff, tableFont=font-1, carouselAutoPlay=false, promoTitleFont=font-2, _styledTemplate=/page/list/PageListH.hbs, ctaButtonText=[], primaryTextColor=#2a2a2a, buttonTextColor=#ffffff, linkTextColor=#1a1a1a, hideTitles=false, footerLinkColor=#ffffff, carouselSpeed=null, buttonHoverBgColor=#a91d23, rteHeadingFont=font-1, secondaryColor=#656565, hideCategories=true, items=[{type=Image, timestamp=1780518265000, category=[{items=[Bears]}], url=https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/03/bears-packers-star-micah-parsons-i-wont-be-back-until-at-least-october-torn-acl, _styledTemplate=null, imageAlignment=null, isFeatured=false, publishDate=June 03, 2026 03:24 PM, media=[{alt=Chicago Bears v Green Bay Packers - entries.title: Festival de El Grito regresará a Grant Park tras la cancelación del año pasado
entries.summary: <p>El festival del centro del Día de la Independencia de México, El Grito, regresará a Grant Park este otoño después de que la celebración del año pasado se puso en pausa debido a preocupaciones sobre la aplicación de la ley de inmigración, anunciaron los organizadores.</p><p>El festival se llevará a cabo en Grant Park el 12 y 13 de septiembre de este año.</p><p>Al igual que muchos eventos de comunidades inmigrantes o internacionales, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/09/05/cancelan-festival-el-grito-en-el-centro-de-chicago-por-posible-actividad-de-ice-y-la-guardia-nacional" target="_blank" >las festividades del año pasado fueron canceladas</a> cuando agentes de inmigración federales detuvieron a miles de personas durante el Operativo Midway Blitz, dejando a muchos inmigrantes en tensión y con miedo de salir de sus hogares.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-570000" name="module-570000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>"Empezamos El Grito Chicago porque creíamos que nuestra comunidad merecía un espacio para celebrar con orgullo quiénes somos. Pausar en 2025 fue doloroso, pero fue un acto de amor", dijo la organizadora Korina Sánchez en el comunicado. "Regresar en 2026 también lo es. No podemos esperar a estar en Grant Park con nuestra gente una vez más".</p><p>El festival contará con presentaciones en vivo, puestos de comida y programación cultural que se anunciarán.</p><p>El Grito, tradicionalmente conocido como el Grito de Dolores, se refiere al discurso de Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla en el que instaba a las personas a luchar por la independencia de México.</p><p>"El Grito de Independencia no es solo un grito histórico de unidad, es una tradición viva que nos recuerda quiénes somos y la fuerza que obtenemos de nuestra herencia compartida", afirmó Reyna Torres Mendivil, Cónsul General de México en Chicago.</p><p>Las entradas con precios de preventa están disponibles en <a class="Link" href="https://www.elgritochicago.com" target="_blank" >elgritochicago.com</a>.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Chicago cop faces firing after passing test to join horseback unit while sidelined with 'unbearable' injury
entries.summary: <p>David Ross passed the strenuous test to join the Chicago Police Department’s mounted patrol in 2023 — successfully climbing onto a horse, lifting five bales of hay and moving a 1,200 pound dumpster.</p><p>The only problem: Officer Ross was on medical leave at the time and was supposed to be recovering from an "unbearable" knee injury sustained during an on-duty crash, police records show.</p><p>Police investigators recommended he be fired for violating the department’s leave policy, according to the city’s Civilian Office of Police Accountability.</p><p>But records show police lawyers are still reviewing the case, and police Supt. Larry Snelling hasn’t filed formal charges seeking Ross’ dismissal. It’s one of at least four disciplinary cases involving Ross that haven’t been finalized.</p><p>Meantime, a newly released COPA report shows he was given a six-month suspension for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2024/08/14/chicago-police-officer-choked-handcuffed-boy-mental-health-crisis-training-new-cop" target="_blank" >choking a boy</a> who was having a mental health episode in 2024.</p><p>A nearly 12-year police veteran, Ross has been named in over a dozen complaints throughout his career, records show.</p><p>He has been relieved of his police powers for nearly two years and has been reassigned to the department’s alternate response section, staffed by cops who have been benched and others not cleared medically for full duty.</p><p>Ross’ lawyer didn’t respond to requests for comment. A police spokesperson declined to comment.</p><h3><b>Back in the saddle</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Ross was injured in the on-duty collision in early 2023, according to a report issued by the police department's internal affairs bureau.</p><p>He tried to go back to work after two days, but the pain in his knee was "unbearable” so he went back on leave, according to the report. A doctor prescribed pain medication and physical therapy.</p><p>Then in March 2023, Ross got a note from another doctor allowing him to participate in the test to join the mounted unit. Around the same time, Ross’ other doctor reported he should remain on medical leave for another month and half.</p><p>Still, Ross completed the physically taxing assessment for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/2/23/18316758/a-pretty-special-horse-that-follows-in-its-master-s-footsteps" target="_blank" >mounted patrol</a> on April 28, 2023. Only about one-third of candidates typically pass, according to the report, and Ross was one of them that year.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-970000" name="image-970000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/643b1e7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1024x575+0+28/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb3%2Ffe%2Fa3653a7250330de15aa3865ea32b%2F492532376-56821683.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7a4d0d9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1024x575+0+28/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb3%2Ffe%2Fa3653a7250330de15aa3865ea32b%2F492532376-56821683.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a23263b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1024x575+0+28/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb3%2Ffe%2Fa3653a7250330de15aa3865ea32b%2F492532376-56821683.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="CHICAGO, IL - OCTOBER 13: The Chicago Police Department Mounted Patrol Unit stands on Clark Street outside of Wrigley Field after the Chicago Cubs beat the St. Louis Cardinals in Game Four to win the National League Divisional Series on October 13, 2015 in Chicago, Illinois. June 27, 2024, Ross was training another cop when he got a call about armed men walking around the West Side.</p><p>When the officers arrived, they found three boys playing with a Nerf gun.</p><p>The officers approached the boys with guns drawn and ordered them up against a fence, COPA said. The toy was found in one of the boys’ waistbands.</p><p>Another boy was wearing a backpack, which Ross believed was concealing a firearm, according to COPA. Ross shoved his gun into the boy's back during a search.</p><p>The boy told Ross that he might as well shoot him, COPA said. Ross then pulled the boy to the ground, straddled him and pressed his fist against the boy’s neck.</p><p>Video shows the boy “gasped for air, made choking noises, and said, ‘I can’t breathe,’” according to COPA. back of a squad car, COPA said. Even as the boy was thrusting himself against the door, making a large banging sound, no one went to check on him.</p><p>The boy was able to move his handcuffs to the front of his body and retrieve a pocket knife from his waistband, slashing a cable for the in-car camera. Then he wrapped a seat belt around his neck, COPA said. </p><p>After about 20 minutes, Ross lowered the window to talk to the boy and found him “lying in a seemingly unconscious state,” according to COPA.</p><p>Ross removed the seat belt from the boy’s neck, pulled him from the car and “dropped him onto the pavement” while still cuffed, COPA said. When the boy regained consciousness, another struggle ensued and Ross again placed his fist against the boy’s throat.</p><p>When questioned by COPA, Ross “firmly denied” putting his fist against the boy's throat while the boy was handcuffed, despite the video evidence, according to the oversight agency.</p><p>The agency found that Ross “took no accountability for his actions and offered numerous excuses and inconsistent explanations in an attempt to justify his misconduct,” which allegedly included using deadly force against a child in handcuffs.</p><p>The oversight agency recommended a suspension for up to a year, but Snelling pushed for the six-month suspension.</p><p>In April, the city’s inspector general’s office urged COPA to reopen that case to investigate whether Ross also filed a false report — a fireable offense.</p><p>COPA declined, saying its investigators had already recommended significant discipline.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2024/08/14/chicago-police-officer-choked-handcuffed-boy-mental-health-crisis-training-new-cop" target="_blank" >Chicago police officer sidelined after choking handcuffed boy having mental health crisis</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/7/23/20707533/memorial-chicago-police-horses-dogs" target="_blank" >Memorial to honor Chicago police horses and dogs who died in the line of duty</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/2/23/18316758/a-pretty-special-horse-that-follows-in-its-master-s-footsteps" target="_blank" >‘A pretty special horse’ that follows in its master’s footsteps</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
