entries.title: Pilsen residents warn of toxic metals from metal scrapper, ask Pritzker to slow permit renewal
entries.summary: <p>Residents living near a large scrap metal operation in Pilsen are asking Gov. JB Pritzker’s administration to tap the brakes on giving the business a new operating permit this year because of fear that it releases too many toxic metals into the air.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/1/13/22882507/pilsen-sims-metal-management-shredder-illinois-environmental-protection-agency" >Sims Metal,</a> which recycles material from junked cars, large appliances and other objects, has been in the crosshairs of federal and state regulators for years. It paid $225,000 to settle a federal environmental case in 2018. And Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/10/22/22741271/pilsen-metal-scrapper-sued-violating-state-pollution-regulations" >sued Sims</a> in 2021, alleging the company didn’t show that it was controlling hazardous air pollution from its operation at 2500 S. Paulina St.</p><p>In an agreement with Raoul, Sims built and installed a new system in April last year that captures air pollution.</p><p>But the Pilsen Environmental Rights and Reform Organization analyzed data that showed an uptick in heavy metals even after the new pollution controls were in place.</p><p>“It’s scary to see these levels,” said Donald Wink, a chemistry professor at the University of Illinois Chicago.</p><p>Tests in 2025 showed an increase in levels of arsenic, cadmium, chromium and other metals, according to Wink’s analysis, which also found that manganese levels were not included in test results.</p><p>At a news conference Wednesday morning, more than two dozen residents and activists held signs and chanted that Sims should be closed, or at the very least further scrutinized, as it recycles hundreds of thousands of tons of metal a year. State officials should require further testing and ask for additional data before giving the company an air pollution operating permit later this year, they said.</p><p>“Who bears the burden of the air pollution from all this activity? Our community,” said Rebeca Ramirez, a lifelong Pilsen resident who said she suffered asthma growing up in the Latino-majority neighborhood.</p><p>At one point, members of the group chanted “Sims es un vecino asesino,” which translates to “Sims is a murderous neighbor.”</p><p>Sims officials dispute the assertions about more metals in the air, saying that federal officials have given the operation a green light, determining that emissions “would not cause either short- or long-term health effects for the community near the facility.”</p><p>“Furthermore, the metals samples from that monitoring effort show further decreases in concentrations after construction of the emission capture and control system earlier in 2025,” Sims said in a statement.</p><p>A spokeswoman for the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency, which is controlled by Pritzker, said she couldn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Sims is a one-of-a-kind metal recycler in Chicago that runs junked cars and other items through a large shredding operation, creating fumes and noise in an industrial area of Pilsen.</p><p>The company’s closest competitor was General Iron, which operated in Lincoln Park for decades until it made plans to move to the Southeast Side and closed its North Side site at the end of 2020. After that company built a new shredding operation at East 116th Street along the Calumet River, Mayor Lori Lightfoot <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/2/18/22940770/southeast-side-metal-shredder-chicago-rejects-plan-open-general-iron-relocation" >decided not to issue a new permit</a> following community protests. That decision is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/02/21/general-iron-lawsuit-seeks-millions-chicago-permit-denial-brandon-johnson-pollution" >still being contested</a> in court.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/1/13/22882507/pilsen-sims-metal-management-shredder-illinois-environmental-protection-agency" >Pilsen metal shredder could become next big environmental battle in Chicago</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/10/22/22741271/pilsen-metal-scrapper-sued-violating-state-pollution-regulations" >Pilsen metal scrapper sued for violating state pollution regulations</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/2/18/22940770/southeast-side-metal-shredder-chicago-rejects-plan-open-general-iron-relocation" >Lightfoot rejects Southeast Side metal shredder’s plan to open</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/02/21/general-iron-lawsuit-seeks-millions-chicago-permit-denial-brandon-johnson-pollution" >General Iron owner seeks millions from City Hall over permit denial</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Programa dará a residentes de Chicago elegibles hasta $70,000 para el enganche de una casa
entries.summary: <p>El alcalde Brandon Johnson y el Departamento de Vivienda de Chicago anunciaron el lunes un nuevo programa que brinda a los residentes de Chicago elegibles hasta $70,000 en asistencia financiera para comprar una nueva casa.</p><p>La subvención HomeGrown Purchase Assistance está dirigida a familias de ingresos bajos y moderados, para quienes ser dueño de casa se está volviendo <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/01/30/affordability-chicago-housing-market-homebuyers-experts-economists" target="_blank" >cada vez más inaccesible</a>. El precio promedio de venta en abril de una casa en Chicago es de $388,918, lo que representa un aumento de más del 5% comparado al año anterior, según Redfin.</p><p>El programa se lanzará el 8 de junio y se espera que ayude a entre 300 y 400 compradores, según el tamaño de cada subvención otorgada.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a60000" name="module-a60000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Como todos sabemos, los precios están aumentando en todas partes, desde la gasolina hasta los alimentos y la propiedad de vivienda”, dijo Destiny Durham, gerente de proyectos de programas para compradores de casa en el Departamento de Vivienda. “Podemos ayudar a los residentes de Chicago a adquirir la casa que desean para que no sientan que está fuera de su alcance porque todo en el clima actual definitivamente está aumentando”.</p><p>El programa de $21 millones está financiado por el bono de desarrollo económico y de vivienda de $1.25 mil millones de Johnson que fue aprobado por el Concejo Municipal en 2024. Durham dijo que se trata de un esfuerzo de financiamiento único para HomeGrown, pero la Municipalidad podría reconsiderar el programa si demuestra ser exitoso.</p><p>Para ser elegibles, los solicitantes deben completar la educación para compradores de vivienda certificada por el Departamento de Vivienda y Desarrollo Urbano (HUD) y estar en condiciones de adquirir una casa unifamiliar o de dos unidades en Chicago que ocuparán durante al menos cinco años como residencia principal.</p><p>El ingreso bruto anual del hogar no puede superar el 150% del ingreso promedio del área, según HUD. Una familia de cuatro con un ingreso del 150% del Ingreso Promedio del Área (AMI) tendría un ingreso anual de $182,250. Un individuo con un ingreso de hasta $127,650 podría calificar.</p><p>Los compradores pueden recibir hasta $70,000 para el pago inicial (enganche) y los costos de cierre, dependiendo de la ubicación de su nueva casa. Para el programa, el departamento clasificó los vecindarios en dos zonas: la Zona A es para áreas que han visto aumentos significativos en los precios de venta de viviendas, y la Zona B abarca áreas de tramos del Censo de bajos ingresos donde el 70% o más de las familias tienen ingresos por debajo del 80% del ingreso familiar promedio estatal.</p><p>Los compradores que adquieran viviendas en la Zona A son elegibles para hasta $70,000 en financiamiento de subvenciones, según sus ingresos. Aquellos que compren viviendas en la Zona B pueden recibir hasta $50,000, según el departamento de vivienda de la ciudad.</p><p>Durham mencionó a Lincoln Park y Lake View como vecindarios incluidos en la Zona A, mientras que la Zona B incluye vecindarios como Englewood y Roseland. Un nuevo sitio web para el programa permitirá a los compradores potenciales ver en qué zona se encuentra la casa que desean, dijo Durham.</p><p>Durham explicó que el departamento decidió hacer HomeGrown un programa a nivel ciudad porque ayudará a reducir la brecha de asequibilidad entre vecindarios y entre compradores.</p><p>“No queremos que la propiedad de vivienda siga siendo inaccesible para muchas familias trabajadoras”, dijo Durham. “Tenemos muchas que podrían quedar fuera por el aumento de costos y también cuentan con una asistencia limitada para el pago inicial. Este [programa] puede ayudar con ambos aspectos”.</p><p>La Municipalidad ofrece otros programas de asistencia para compradores de vivienda como TaxSmart, programa de Certificado de Crédito Hipotecario que otorga a los compradores de casa por primera vez, o a aquellos que compran en un “tramo del Censo económicamente problemático”, un crédito fiscal reclamable por una parte de su pago anual de interés hipotecario. Pero Durham dijo que HomeGrown es único porque es a nivel ciudad y otorga más financiamiento que otros programas. Las subvenciones tampoco se limitan a viviendas de nueva construcción, a diferencia de algunos otros programas de la ciudad.</p><p>“Esto será para propiedades existentes en toda la ciudad de Chicago, donde queremos reducir la brecha de asequibilidad y permitir que los ciudadanos de Chicago accedan a ser dueños de vivienda asequible”, agregó.</p><p>Neighborhood Lending Services y TRP Lending, una filial del Proyecto Resurrección, administrarán el programa, según el departamento de vivienda.</p><p>“Queremos que los residentes de Chicago puedan permitirse criar a sus hijos y vivir sus vidas en nuestra ciudad”, dijo Johnson en un comunicado de prensa. “A medida que trabajamos para invertir en oportunidades de vivienda y expandir los caminos hacia una vivienda estable y asequible para todos nuestros residentes, es un objetivo clave de nuestra administración asegurar que la propiedad de vivienda siga siendo accesible para las familias trabajadoras de Chicago, mientras invertimos en la riqueza generacional, estabilidad comunitaria y oportunidades a largo plazo en cada comunidad”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Just like he did with Astros, Alex Bregman making presence felt with behind-the-scenes impact for Cubs
entries.summary: <p>Alex Bregman is a lot of things.</p><p>He’s a Gold Glove third baseman. He’s a Silver Slugger at the plate.</p><p>He’s an All Star. He’s a World Series champion. He’s the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ $175 million man.</p><p>But he’s also, sometimes, an impromptu pitching coach.</p><p>“He’s an outstanding resource, not only for our position players but also for our pitchers. Just an extremely high baseball IQ guy,” relief pitcher Phil Maton told the Sun-Times on Wednesday. “I don’t know if anyone truly puts in more work off the field with scouting than he does. He’s coming in here giving me scouting reports for how to pitch guys.</p><p>“I’m like, ‘I don’t even know how you had time to do that. You’ve got to prepare to hit against 13 arms.’ And he’s over here like, ‘You need to do this to this guy if you face him.’</p><p>“If he sees something that might help our pitchers, I think it’s great he’s telling guys, ‘This is what I see.’ It might make a big out in a game today.”</p><p>While descriptive of Bregman’s behind-the-scenes impact, that anecdote will only go so far toward swaying the opinions of frustrated fans who might not think Bregman is living up to his contract. The Cubs are <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/02/cubs-losing-streak-may-june-colin-rea-pete-crow-armstrong-leadoff-craig-counsell-lineup" >in the middle of a nasty stretch</a>, coming into Wednesday losers of 17 of their last 22.</p><p>The offense has looked broken, and the lack of power production from Bregman is among the concerns. He only hit five homers and drove in 19 runs in his first 60 games as a Cub. He’s also been one of the few productive Cubs hitters of late, hitting .303 with a .361 on-base percentage over his final 18 games in May, a stretch that included an 11-game hit streak.</p><p>But Bregman stepped into his Cubs tenure as more than just a bat. He brought with him a reputation as a strong clubhouse presence, and the reviews are as good as anyone could have hoped for.</p><p>“He can’t wait for the next day to come, good or bad,” manager Craig Counsell said. “That’s never going to change with Alex. That’s just who he is.</p><p>“He’s mad when the game’s over. Even if he’s having a bad game, he’s upset the game’s over. He’d like to keep playing. That’s just who he is. That’s a great trait, and I think everybody feels it.”</p><p>Maton has seen this before. He and Bregman were Astros teammates for three years, a stretch that included a World Series win in 2021.</p><p>Now Maton is seeing it again, and it’s impressing him even more this time.</p><p>“Honestly, I think he’s grown a little bit more,” Maton said. “We had a really good clubhouse in Houston, we had a lot of guys. I don’t know if this is [what happened] when he went to Boston or when he came here, but he’s really grown into just becoming ‘the guy.’”</p><p>Bregman’s status as the player who got the Cubs to finally shell out big free-agent bucks brings the expectations that he will be “the guy” for this team.</p><p>Maton believes that’s coming – “I know it’s going to turn for him, I don’t question that for a second” – and in addition to speaking from the experience of playing alongside him, he can speak from the experience of trying to get Bregman out.</p><p>The two have only faced off twice, most recently last season, when Maton induced a Bregman ground out. But the first time, Bregman struck with a walk-off single in extra innings.</p><p>“Even when he’s not producing at the level he’d like to be at, he’s always a tough at-bat,” Maton said. “[Even] when he’s going through it, you have to go out there and beat him in the zone. And that’s something that creates a ton of value. It puts a ton of pressure on the other team.</p><p>“I’m glad he’s on our side and I don’t have to deal with him this year.”</p><p>The Cubs hope headaches like that start piling up for opposing pitchers.</p><p>But no matter the on-field results, it seems the Cubs are getting what they paid for behind the scenes.</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 entries.title: SpaceX's IPO is set to be the biggest ever and could make Elon Musk world's first trillionaire
entries.summary: <p>SpaceX says it plans to raise up to $75 billion when it goes public this month, setting the stage for the largest-ever stock market debut and putting Elon Musk on course to becoming the world's first trillionaire.</p><p>The company, formally known as Space Exploration Technologies Corp., said Wednesday it will sell 555.6 million shares at $135 a piece in an initial public offering. The estimated proceeds would easily top the $26 billion raised by oil giant Saudi Aramco in 2019. The offering would also give SpaceX a market value of $1.77 trillion. Only six companies in the S&P 500 are currently worth more, with Nvidia tops at $5.2 trillion.</p><p>Besides the size of the offering and the expected proceeds, SpaceX’s amended prospectus updates details about how much control Musk will have over the company. As SpaceX’s CEO, chief technical officer and chairman, Musk’s voting power will come primarily through his ownership of 5.22 billion Class B shares, which give the holder 10 votes for every share. Musk would have 82.4% of the voting power, according to the filing.</p><p>Forbes currently values Musk's net worth at $826 billion and his stake in SpaceX at $542 billion. The estimated value of his SpaceX holdings was based on an overall value for the company of $1.25 trillion. Based on those numbers, a $1.77 trillion valuation for SpaceX would boost Musk’s net worth by $223 billion, making him a trillionaire. However, much of Musk's worth is in stock that he has yet to cash in.</p><p>Even as it makes a bid for a blockbuster market debut, SpaceX is currently losing billions of dollars a year. The filing shows that the company lost $2.6 billion from operations last year on $18.7 billion in revenue, and the losses kept piling up at the start of this year, too.</p><p>Time will tell how SpaceX fares on the market. Musk’s plans for the company are as fantastical as the money he hopes to raise in the sale.</p><p>Colorful, <a class="Link" href="https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1181412/000162828026040364/spaceexplorationtechnologib.htm" target="_blank" >even frightening in parts</a>, the IPO document strikes a contrast with the typically dry, technical prose in IPO documents — detailing plans to use proceeds from the sale to help put men on the moon again and perhaps even Mars. One section talks of a need to build “a permanent human colony” on the red planet with “at least one million inhabitants” as existential threats loom that could consign man to “the same fate as the dinosaurs.”</p><p>Musk has almost equally ambitious plans for his other publicly traded company, Tesla. His goal is to transform the maker of electric vehicles into a producer of robotaxis and humanoid robots. Dan Ives, of Wedbush Securities, wrote in a research note that he expects Tesla and SpaceX to merge next year.</p><p>Key to the success of both companies — and any merged entity — is artificial intelligence. In its IPO filing, SpaceX says it sees potential revenue from AI of up to $26.5 trillion. But that depends on another lofty Musk ambition — putting data centers in space, which is not technologically possible at the moment.</p><p>Transforming his space company into a primarily AI-focused company will be a challenge for Musk, who started xAI in 2023 with 11 other co-founders who have all since left. Some were recruited away by rivals.</p><p>Its main AI product, the chatbot Grok, is “less impressive than anything that we see from any other major player in the space, whether that’s OpenAI, or Anthropic, or (Google’s) Gemini,” IDC analyst Arnal Dayaratna said.</p><p>Dayaratna said that doesn’t mean SpaceX doesn’t have potential as a major AI player, thanks in part to its computing partnership with Anthropic and Musk’s recent deal that gave SpaceX the rights to buy AI coding tool Cursor for $60 billion later this year. Folding in Cursor’s capabilities would give SpaceX access to the coveted business customers now using Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT.</p><p>SpaceX plans to use the net proceeds from the IPO to fund the expansion of infrastructure for its AI and rocket businesses and to beef up the constellation of satellites that power Starlink Mobile, among other investments.</p><p>The company plans to list on the Nasdaq under the symbol “SPCX” and could begin trading as soon as the end of next week.</p><p>SpaceX isn’t the only colossal market debut investors are now bracing for. Earlier this week, Anthropic submitted a confidential filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission to officially start its own IPO clock.</p><p>OpenAI has not yet reported filing the initial SEC paperwork, but an IPO from the ChatGPT maker is widely expected.</p><p>“This listing represents the first major test for public markets after years of muted IPO activity with SpaceX paving the way for AI giants Anthropic and OpenAI to follow soon after,” Ives wrote.</p>

entries.title: United Center owners break ground on their $7 billion 1901 Project
entries.summary: <p>Construction has started on the 1901 Project — signaling the transformation of what's been described as a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/07/23/united-center-reinsdorf-wirtz-1901-project-housing-entertainment-hall-retail-campus-arena" >“sea of parking lots”</a> around the United Center with what officials call the largest private investment on the Near West Side.</p><p>The United Center's owners, the Wirtz and Reinsdorf families, and elected officials held a groundbreaking ceremony on Wednesday for the $7 billion privately funded project. </p><p>The multiphase project will create an estimated 2,400 construction jobs and thousands of permanent jobs over its lifetime.</p><div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Rendering of the 1901 Project’s Music Hall and West Park, which will have recreational courts, open space and community programming.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided by RIOS</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Despite its size, the project's timeline has moved relatively fast compared to other sports-centered projects in Chicago. United Center's leaders unveiled the 1901 Project in July 2024, and in February 2025, it was unanimously approved by the City Council. In May, the council approved a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/05/20/city-council-tax-break-united-center-entertainment-district" >$54.7 million property tax break</a> for the project’s first phase.</p><p>Under Cook County’s Class 7b special assessment, the project’s property tax rate for phase one will be 10% for the first 10 years, 15% for year 11 then 20% for year 12.</p><p>The 1901 Project’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/01/16/first-phase-united-center-7b-redevelopment-approved-plan-commission" target="_blank" ><u>first phase</u></a> is valued at $500 million. Projects must be valued at $2 million or more to be eligible for Class 7b incentives.</p><p>Johnson has defended the United Center subsidy, and is a strong supporter of the project. He said Wednesday the 1901 Project’s emphasis on arts, culture and community will help the site become an economic engine for the city — and nearby residents.</p><p>“This is an investment that will create jobs and housing, attract new businesses, generate economic activity and help ensure that the benefits of growth reach the residents and families who call the West Side home,” he said.</p><p>Department of Planning and Development Commissioner Ciere Boatright said it's an “inclusionary approach” to development. United Center's owners have emphasized hiring locally for construction jobs. The nonprofit 1901 Community Implementation Committee was created to bring community members into the fold and give them the skills needed to eventually become subcontractors on the project.</p><p>One of the community leaders working in coordination on the project was Jerry Lewis, executive director of the 1901 Community Implementation Committee. Lewis, 67, of Matteson, was killed in an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/27/chicago-crime-jerry-lewis-united-center-shooting" >apparent assassination attempt</a> in March outside of the nonprofit’s office at 2127 W. Madison St., near the United Center.</p><p>Ald. Walter R. Burnett (27th) said Lewis deserves recognition for the role he played in helping to shape the community and the 1901 Project.</p><p>“Jerry believed deeply in the power of community,” Burnett said. “He believed that the development should create opportunity for those who already live here. His passing was a tremendous loss, but his vision and his values are embedded in this project, and his legacy will live on in what we create here together.”</p><p>The master plan for the land around the United Center emerged after five years of planning, Terry Savarise, United Center's executive vice president and CEO, previously said. It was stewarded by White Sox Chairman Jerry Reinsdorf and the late Blackhawks Chairman <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2023/7/25/23807793/rocky-wirtz-dies-blackhawks-chairman-bill-danny-wirtz-breakthru-beverage" target="_blank" >Rocky Wirtz</a>, who died in 2023. </p><p>Some pieces of the plan, including a new <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/09/27/1901-project-united-center-mega-development-walter-burnett-pink-line-station" >Pink Line L station</a>, are still coming together. Boatright said a Pink Line station on Paulina Street is “closer to a reality,” as conversations between the project team and city progress.</p><p>Blackhawks Chairman and CEO Danny Wirtz said the energy inside the United Center is “unlike anything we see in the city,” but it has been confined inside the arena's walls. The 1901 Project will remove that vacuum and bring more energy and investment to the West Side, he said.</p><p>“This project is … a commitment to the people who've been here all along. That energy and investment flowing into this campus now flows through the neighborhood and not just around it,” Wirtz said. “We are building with this community and not just near it.”</p><div entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams' giant leap will require one from WR Rome Odunze as well
entries.summary: <p>If <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams truly is on his way to the moon this season, wide receiver Rome Odunze needs to be the rocket booster that helps him get there.</p><p>Odunze has been fine his first two seasons, but he aspires for more than that and the Bears expected more when they drafted him ninth overall in 2024. Teams hope they’re landing a perennial All-Pro in that range, and the Bears certainly envisioned that when they took Williams and Odunze in the top 10.</p><p>While Williams’ arrow was indisputably pointed upwardly at the end of last season, the outlook on Odunze wasn’t so clear. He suffered a stress fracture in his right foot early in the season, missed five games and was hindered by the injury in others. He finished fourth on the team in catches (44), third in yards (661) and tied for first in touchdowns (six).</p><p>Decent numbers, but again, No. 9 picks need to be better than that. If Williams hadn’t been the No. 1 pick in that same class, there’d be a lot more heat on Odunze at this stage.</p><p>He didn’t crack the top 25 in catches, yards or touchdowns last season, and among wide receivers in his draft class, he’s sixth in catches and fifth in yards and touchdowns through two seasons. The intense spotlight on Williams has given him some cover.</p><p>As Odunze heads into a pivotal season, both from the Bears’ perspective as they usher him fully into the No. 1 receiver role after trading DJ Moore and from his own as he vies for a major contract extension, the picture remains cloudy.</p><p>Not only has Odunze yet to prove he’s a true No. 1 threat — “I truly believe I can be one of the best in the league, so until I go out there and do that, I’m not satisfied,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/02/07/you-either-do-or-you-dont-bears-wr-rome-odunze-harsh-critic-of-himself-despite-improvement" >he told the Sun-Times in February</a> — but he also indicated Wednesday his foot simply isn’t going to be what it was before the injury.</p><p>Odunze laughed when asked if there was a point in the offseason when he felt back to “normal” running on his foot and said there’s no such thing.</p><p>“This is my new normal,” he said. “It’s not from a standpoint that I’m always in pain but the way my foot broke... creates a different type of foot structure with those bones — different types of things that kind of shift things around.</p><p>“I don’t think that’s anything that’s going to prohibit me from making plays but ... it’s never really back to ‘normal.’”</p><p>Odunze was confident about his future nonetheless, and coach Ben Johnson said Wednesday, “He looks pretty good right now,” but there’s a long way to go to the season opener, let alone the 17-game schedule.</p><p>That’s certainly a concern worth monitoring, but setting it aside for the moment, Odunze has a lot of work to do even if he stays healthy.</p><p>No matter what Johnson says about the Bears being stacked with playmakers, every quarterback needs a game-changing wide receiver. When Johnson was with the Lions, they gave Jared Goff a dynamic weapon in Amon-Ra St. Brown. Just this week, the Patriots found that type of wide receiver for quarterback Drake Maye, who went two picks behind Williams in 2024, by trading for Eagles six-time 1,000-yard receiver A.J. Brown.</p><p>The Bears’ swing at finding someone like that was using a premium draft pick on Odunze.</p><p>Everything from his and Williams’ rookie season is a tangled mess, and it’s hard to make much of an evaluation on him amid the dysfunction under former coach Matt Eberflus and Williams’ ups and downs that year.</p><p>Odunze sharpened his route running under Johnson last season, but his chemistry with Williams was still shaky and his hands weren’t as reliable as they should be. Odunze officially had only three drops — one that would’ve been a touchdown against the Rams in the playoffs — but there were other balls he felt he should’ve caught.</p><p>Of the 90 passes thrown to Odunze in the regular season, he caught just 48.9% — 73rd among the 78 players at his position who got at least 50 targets. It didn’t help that Williams had accuracy problems and finished last in completion percentage (58.1) and second-to-last in on-target throws (69.8), so they share blame.</p><p>Odunze said preoccupation with pain in his foot sometimes affected his concentration and he struggled to adapt to playing while hurt, but that didn’t excuse any lapses. As he said in February, “In this league, you either do or you don’t.”</p><p>While Williams draws the bulk of the attention, the Bears are watching Odunze closely. With Moore gone, it’s time for him to take the lead, and it’s hard to envision Williams taking the next step without Odunze taking one, too.</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Joel Moorman</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><ul id="rte-8c4015a0-5ad5-11f1-aeb5-b903bf09aeab"><li>Steppenwolf ensemble member Gary Cole returns to the Chicago stage for the first time in 25 years to join fellow ensemble members (Audrey Francis, Tim Hopper and director Amy Morton) in a production of <b>“Catch as Catch Can,”</b> Mia Chung’s play in which three actors take on six roles in a story about a prodigal son who returns and sets off a spiraling crisis for two families. Sarah Charipar is also in the cast. From June 4-July 12 at Steppenwolf Theatre, 1650 N. Halsted St. Tickets: $20-$120. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://steppenwolf.org" target="_blank" ><u>steppenwolf.org</u></a>.</li><li><b>“Leopoldstadt”</b> is late playwright Tom Stoppard’s final work, an epic masterpiece that follows a Jewish family as its members brave the darkest and most consequential chapters of the 20th century. Featuring a 29-member cast, it’s the largest production in Writers Theatre history. Carey Perloff, a frequent Stoppard collaborator, directs. From June 4-July 19 at Writers Theatre, 325 Tudor Ct., Glencoe. Tickets: $55-$125. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://writerstheatre.org" target="_blank" ><u>writerstheatre.org</u></a>.</li><li>Kevin Douglas’ new romantic-comedy-meets-horror story, <b>“Untitled Vampire Play,”</b> explores love, commitment, codependency and, of course, vampires. Devon DeMayo directs. From June 4-July 12 at Lookingglass Theatre, Water Tower Water Works, 163 E. Pearson St. Tickets: $33+. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://lookingglasstheatre.org" target="_blank" ><u>lookingglasstheatre.org</u></a>.</li><li>Cyndi Lauper and Harvey Fierstein’s Tony Award-winning musical <b>“Kinky Boots”</b> follows the story of a shoe factory owner, trying to save his business, who finds inspiration in Lola, a fabulous entertainer in need of some sturdy stilettos. From June 9-21 at Nederlander Theatre, 24 W. Randolph St. Tickets: $49-$126. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://broadwayinchicago.com" target="_blank" ><u>broadwayinchicago.com</u></a>.</li><li>In the musical comedy, <b>“Nunsense,”</b> the nuns from the Little Sisters of Hoboken stage a variety show fundraiser filled with musical numbers and comedy. E. Faye Butler directs. From June 10-Aug. 2 at Drury Lane Theatre, 100 Drury Lane, Oakbrook Terrace. Tickets: $85-$150. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://drurylanetheatre.com" target="_blank" ><u>drurylanetheatre.com</u></a>.</li><li><b>“Two Out of Three Falls”</b> is Bill Daniel’s drama about a daughter seeking to avenge her wrestling legend father’s murder. Ashley Yates directs. From June 4-July 18 at The Factory Theater, 1623 W. Howard St. Tickets: $30. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://thefactorytheater.com" target="_blank" ><u>thefactorytheater.com</u></a>.</li><li><b>“Smiley,” </b>a queer romantic comedy by Spanish playwright Guillem Clua, revolves around a love story between two men who meet because of a misdirected voicemail. Jack Dugan Carpenter directs. From June 5-21 at Open Space Arts, 1411 W. Wilson Ave. Tickets: $30. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://openspacearts.org" target="_blank" ><u>openspacearts.org</u></a>.</li><li>Jason Robert Brown’s musical, <b>“The Last Five Years,”</b> follows a romantic relationship over half a decade as a couple falls in and out of love. entries.title: Sam Antonacci reaches base all six times up, sparking White Sox in rout of Twins
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox </a>left fielder Sam Antonacci has been a spark plug at the top of the order against right-handers. In the Sox’ 8-0 victory Wednesday against the Twins, he recorded his fourth multihit game in his last eight.</p><p>But he took that even further, reaching base all six times he came to the plate. Antonacci went 4-for-4 with a walk and his 12th hit-by-pitch of the season, tied for the most in baseball. How does he do it?</p><p>“He’s just crazy,” said Sox first baseman Jacob Gonzalez, who played with Antonacci in the minors. “Not that he’s playing recklessly, but he plays crazy. Stretching [singles into] doubles, but everyone wants to do that. It’s just that he’s also fast enough to be able to do crazy things. It’s a lot of fun.”</p><p>“Just got a lot of good pitches to hit today and got on base,” Antonacci said in the understatement of the day.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Sam Antonacci's third hit of the day brings the <a href="https://x.com/whitesox?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@whitesox</a> lead to 5⃣ <a href="https://t.co/9manCdNUDF">pic.twitter.com/9manCdNUDF</a></p>— White Sox on CHSN (@CHSN_WhiteSox) <a href="https://x.com/CHSN_WhiteSox/status/2062252909329330609?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">June 3, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>He had two doubles, two runs and an RBI. His 13 multihit games are tied for second-most on the team. But he claims it has nothing to do with batting leadoff.</p><p>“It’s the same wherever you’re hitting,” Antonacci said. “Seeing the same ball, getting the same pitches. Doesn’t change my mindset. Just trying to get on base for the people behind me.”</p><p>One of those people is Gonzalez, who went 2-for-4 for his first career multihit game. He also recorded his first two career RBI on a bases-loaded single in the first inning, when the Sox scored four runs.</p><p>It was more than enough for starter Erick Fedde, who didn’t allow a hit until there were two outs in the fifth, and the bullpen. Fedde ended up allowing two hits in five innings before Grant Taylor and Chris Murphy completed the shutout.</p><p>But the win might’ve had a cost. After entering the game in right field in the seventh, Derek Hill got hit by a pitch on his left hand in the ninth. He felt good enough to stay in the game — the Sox had no other outfielders on the bench — but he went for imaging after the game and his hand was heavily wrapped in ice.</p><h3>Mune wins May rookie award</h3><p>Munetaka Murakami isn’t traveling with the Sox as he recovers from a strained right hamstring, but he still made news by being named the American League Rookie of the Month for May.</p><p>“Love that for him, and I love that for us,” Venable said. “So proud of him for the work he’s put in and the performance on the field. He’s very well deserving of that award. He’s contributed in every way possible at the highest level.”</p><p>Murakami slashed .244/.382/.556 with eight home runs, 18 RBI, 21 runs and 19 walks in 26 games in May. He led all rookies for the month in homers, runs and walks, tied for the lead in RBI and ranked second in slugging percentage and OPS (.937).</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>Shortstop Colson Montgomery returned to the lineup after being given most of the game Tuesday off. He entered as a pinch hitter in the seventh inning and got hit by a pitch. Venable said he was no worse for wear.</p><p>“It was really a bummer on a day where we’re trying to give him some rest that he comes in and takes one off the knee,” Venable said. “But he’s all right. He’s a young guy that has good, strong bones.”</p><p>• Left-hander Noah Schultz isn’t scheduled to throw another bullpen session as he recovers from tendinitis in his right knee.</p><p>“No decision on that,” Venable said. “There’s still some soreness in there, so they backed off to give him a little bit of a blow and then ramp back up.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true"
